# A brief history of the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup

29 January, 2026

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.icc-cricket.com%2Fmedia-releases%2Fa-brief-history-of-the-icc-men-s-t20-world-cup)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.icc-cricket.com%2Fmedia-releases%2Fa-brief-history-of-the-icc-men-s-t20-world-cup&text=A%20brief%20history%20of%20the%20ICC%20Men%E2%80%99s%20T20%20World%20Cup)

![Image 18: Carlos Brathwaite 'Remember the Moment' Six | Bira Six Days of Sixes](link_42)

**Media release**

We are now nearly two decades removed from the introduction of the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup, which ushered in a new era for the game when India emerged victorious from that thrilling 2007 tournament in South Africa.

There were 12 teams competing in that inaugural outing, while there will be 20 teams from all corners of the globe competing to win the tournament’s 10th edition in 2026. Six different teams have lifted the trophy over the years, with the West Indies, England and reigning champions India the only nations to have won it twice.

Ahead of the 2026 tournament in India and Sri Lanka, let’s take a little trip down memory lane.

**A new form of cricket**

The 21st century has stood witness to the emergence of T20 cricket as one of sport’s fastest growing formats, but there was major scepticism when it was first mooted around English county cricket circles.

Initially seen as a way to attract new people to the sport and simplify the game to wider audiences, T20 cricket has transformed the game’s landscape since first being introduced at the professional level in 2003 and then quickly adopted around the world.

The birth of the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup in 2007 took it to another level and that tournament’s impact was immediate.

Legendary West Indian Chris Gayle was responsible for that, sending the very first ball of the tournament to the fence before smashing a remarkable 117 against the hosts – making the first ever T20I century in the process.

From bowl-outs to Yuvraj Singh taking six sixes off one Stuart Broad over and Misbah-ul-Haq’s infamous scoop in the final, that first tournament proved an historic first edition.

Culminating in India’s stunning victory over Pakistan, it not only set a new course for the modern game but also the tone for the drama that would follow at ICC Men’s T20 World Cups in the decades to follow.

**Iconic moments**

Pakistan avenged their loss to India by claiming victory in 2009, as Shahid Afridi, a player born for the format, shone with both bat and ball in England. The tournament also saw the hosts stunned by the Netherlands in one of the all-time great upsets.

England responded a year later in the Caribbean by winning their first men’s white-ball trophy as Kevin Pietersen earned Player of the Tournament honours for his efforts with the bat.

Then in 2012, West Indies joined the party by triumphing in Sri Lanka, with Marlon Samuels (78) and Sunil Narine (3-9) the stars of the show in the final.

They beat the hosts to lift the trophy that year, but Sri Lanka bounced back by winning in 2014 to ensure Kumar Sangakkara and Mahela Jayawardene bowed out of the format in style.

The West Indies were back on top of the world two years later thanks to Carlos Brathwaite’s four consecutive sixes off Ben Stokes in the last over of the 2016 final in Kolkota, a moment etched in cricket’s collective memory thanks Ian Bishop’s immortal “remember the name” call on commentary.

After a five-year absence, the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup resumed in 2021 as Australia claimed their first title. David Warner and Mitchell Marsh were the heroes in the final against New Zealand.

A year later, it was England who triumphed for a second time, ensuring they held both the T20 and ODI world titles. Sam Curran stole the show that year and was both named Player of the Match in the final and Player of the Tournament for his all-round contributions.

**Going global**

In 2024, the tournament expanded from 16 teams to 20, with the USA, Canada and Uganda making their debuts.

The Americans, co-hosting alongside the West Indies, seized their opportunity with a stunning Super Over victory over Pakistan as they progressed to the Super 8 stage. Afghanistan also enjoyed a dream run, making it to the semi-finals of a major ICC tournament for the first time.

Virat Kohli saved his best for last in the final with 76, but that did not look like it would be enough until a magical spell from Jasprit Bumrah derailed South Africa’s chase and set up an seven-run victory for India.

As with Sangakkara and Jayawardene a decade earlier, this proved to be a final farewell for two modern greats as Kohli and Rohit Sharma both called time on their international T20 careers.

That means new faces in 2026, and another new team in Italy, who will look to hit the ground running when they make their World Cup debut in India and Sri Lanka.

# Bossaball: The World‘s Newest Competitive Sport

![Image 3](https://expertbeacon.com/wp-content/uploads/avatars/2893/1731561064-bpthumb.jpg)By James Dorn Last Update on May 13, 2024

As a passionate gamer and gaming industry expert, I analyze the latest and hottest sports both on screen and off. And one new sport bursting onto the global scene is bossaball. **Bossaball, originating in 2004, is the newest competitive team sport in the world** – and its high-flying blend of volleyball, soccer and gymnastics is capturing attention everywhere from Europe to Asia.

## My Background Evaluating Cutting-Edge Games

As a gaming content creator for over a decade, I’ve built a reputation for identifying rising stars in the interactive entertainment world – whether eSports, live-action roleplaying games or inventive new physical sports that leverage technology. I evaluate these sports’ mass appeal, global growth potential and possible Olympic candidacy.

Bossaball demonstrates tremendous promise in all facets. The visionary concept of Filip Eyckmans, bossaball strategically merges the explosive pace of volleyball with nimble footwork inspired by soccer and jaw-dropping acrobatics akin to gymnasts. This intersection of established sports played upon a bouncy court featuring trampolines on either side of the net creates sheer spectacle. The athleticism required to strike a ball mid-air while coordinating team formations introduces skilful complexity absent from most traditional sports.

## Bossaball Court Set-Up and Rule Highlights

Bossaball is contested between two teams of 4 or 5 players on a 10 by 20 meter inflatable court. Users may employ hands, feet or head – as in soccer‘s heading – to pass and strike the ball.

*   Teams alternate contacts with the ball across the net, up to 3 touches allowed per possession
*   Players jump from trampolines integrated along each sideline for gravity-defying spikes, blocks and digs 
*   Controlled net contact expands volley exchanges not seen in volleyball
*   Up to two player substitutions per team per set 

Matches consist of best 3-out-of-5 sets rally scored to 25 points, winning by a two point margin. Bossaball sessions also uniquely integrate music and lighting effects to punctuate epic rallies, further energizing the crowd.

## Recent Bossaball Growth Statistics

While originally founded in Belgium, bossaball‘s headquarters shifted to Barcelona, Spain given passionate European adoption. As of 2023:

*   **450+ bossaball courts** across **47 countries** worldwide and 6 continents
*   Approximtely **8-10 new countries** add bossaball courts annually 
*   Brazil, Spain, France and Slovakia home to most thriving national pro leagues 
*   **35% participation growth in North America** from 2021 to 2022
*   2024 debut as **demonstration sport at Asia Games** and 2028 **Central American/Caribbean Games**

## Projecting Bossaball‘s Future Appeal

While alternatives like spikeball and bubble soccer gain momentary notoriety, both lack bossaball‘s creative foundations in popular sports to enable sustained mainstream appeal. Volleyball and soccer aficionados will recognize familiar gameplay elements while dazzling aerial acrobatics attract wider entertainment seekers.

As international growth rates demonstrate, I project bossaball cementing itself alongside established games like rugby or lacrosse over the next decade. Innovative adoption as a demonstration event in leading competitions like the Asia Games foreshadows full medal status. And bossaball’s accessibility regardless of age, gender or body type strengthens its case as an Olympic dark horse candidate.

Given relentless digital immersion today, spectator sports guaranteeing live thrills will only increase in value – and bossaball promises those in spades. Its vibrant merging of team dynamics, live music and physics-defying stunts make bossaball set to become _the_ trending sport for 2025 and beyond!

## What is a Crossword Clue?

According to [The New York Times](link_35), a crossword clue is “a hint that the solver must decipher to find the answer that is then entered into the puzzle grid.” Depending on the puzzle type, clues can range from synonyms to definitions, from puns to wordplay and from general knowledge to fill-in-the-blanks. The possibilities are endless.

If you already have an answer to a clue, use the Crossword Clue tool above to search for clues that have the same answer.

## What is a Crossword Answer?

When you solve for a clue, the resulting word or phrase is the answer, sometimes called a “fill”. Fills can range from one word to multiple words. When you have solved for all clues in a puzzle, all of the answers contribute to a completed puzzle.

If you’re stuck on a crossword clue and can’t decipher and answer, don’t worry! Plug your clue into the [Crossword Solver](https://www.wordplays.com/crossword-solver/) to search through millions of clue/answer pairs for a possible solution.

## Crossword Construction

Would you like to create your own crossword puzzles? Whether you’re a teacher, a crossword enthusiast or just having some fun, the Crossword Clue tool is the perfect sidekick for crossword constructing. Enter a word or phrase into the search box to generate a list of clues with that same answer. Use the results as inspiration for creating your own clues. You’ll be an expert compiler in no time!

Check out the [Crossword Solver](https://www.wordplays.com/crossword-solver/) to search for clues with different answers.

To create a crossword puzzle on Wordplays.com, use the [Crossword Puzzle Maker](link_36).

## Learn Crosswordese

Crosswordese is a group of words used by puzzle constructors to add more vowels to the board. These range from abbreviations to fictional cartoon characters, or from brand names to latin phrases. As you continue through your solving journey, you’ll begin to familiarize yourself with some of the most common Crosswordese. Here are some of our favorites:

SMEE (Mr. Smee is a fictional character who serves as Captain Hook's boatswain or a small compact diving duck)

Clues that contain SMEE:

*   [Right-hand man for a man with no right hand](link_37)
*   [Ducks out of bosses meeting](link_38)
*   Captain Hook’s sidekick yells “duck!”

IRA (A man’s name, or an Individual Retirement Account)

Clues that contain IRA:

*   [Man's name has a certain air about it](link_39)
*   [Part of a nest egg, in brief](link_40)
*   [Investment alternative to a 401(k): Abbr.](https://www.wordplays.com/crossword-solver/Investment-alternative-to-a-401%28k%29%3A-Abbr [link_41].)

ALI (Boxing legend or Folktale hero)

## What is 100% Cricket?

##### 100% Cricket is an authentic platform that aims to change perceptions, create heroes and excitement, and support women in cricket. The campaign aims to increase the visibility and engagement of women’s cricket during and outside ICC Events, positioning women’s cricket as a viable sustainable commercial platform and reinforce ICC’s position at the forefront of the global women’s sport movement.

##### Women's cricket is one of the strategic priorities identified by the ICC, with the aim to 'Accelerate the growth of women's cricket, delivering 250 million incremental fans by 2032'.

##### To achieve this, the ICC's Women's Cricket Strategy identifies four action areas: Programmes, Profile, Participation, People.

[![Image 17: 100percent image block](https://images.icc-cricket.com/image/private/t_q-best/v1725557339/prd/assets/100percent_cricket/Women's%20Strategy%204Ps%20ICC%20Brand.jpg)](https://www.icc-cricket.com/100percentcricket/what-is-100percent-cricket#nolink)

##### The 100% Cricket campaign aligns strongly with the Profile and People action areas of the Women's Cricket Strategy. It does so through various projects aimed at increasing the visibility of the women's game, creating female role models that fans can connect with. It also looks to support women working in cricket and create more female leaders.

### Watch this video to learn more about the 100% Cricket campaign:

### What is 100% Cricket?

[![Image 18: Black 100 percent cricket](https://images.icc-cricket.com/image/private/t_ratio16_9-size20-webp/v1722853109/prd/assets/100percent_cricket/blank_100_percent_cricket.svg)](https://www.icc-cricket.com/100percentcricket/what-is-100percent-cricket#nolink)

##### 100% Cricket celebrates everything we love about the game, including players' attitudes, discipline, and abilities. It's about the spectacle of the game played by the best women in the world, celebrating individuals, teams, fans, and spirit. This section explores stories, athletes, and accomplishments, celebrating what it means and takes to be 100% in anything.

# Crossword Solver Help

Solve crossword puzzles using the **Crossword Solver**. Find possible crossword puzzle answers by searching through millions of crossword puzzle clues.

  

#### Crossword Puzzle Answer

Type the crossword puzzle answer into the text field labeled "Enter a Crossword Puzzle Clue". Crossword puzzle clues can be words or phrases of up to 100 characters. Punctuation in a crossword puzzle clue can change the meaning of the clue, so enter punctuation accurately.

#### Optional Answer Pattern

You probably know how long the crossword puzzle answer is and you might even know some of the letters. Help the Crossword Solver find the correct answer by entering a pattern that describes the answer. Use a '?' to represent an unknown letter.

#### Pattern Example

**Pattern****Result**
**????**answer is 4 letters long, no letters are known
**??G**answer length 3 and ends with **G**
**8**answer length is 8, no letters are known
**?A4**answer has 6 letters, 2nd letter is **A**

 Any punctuation mark or space will be replaced with a **?**

# Bossaball: The World‘s Newest Competitive Sport

![Image 3](https://expertbeacon.com/wp-content/uploads/avatars/2893/1731561064-bpthumb.jpg)By James Dorn Last Update on May 13, 2024

As a passionate gamer and gaming industry expert, I analyze the latest and hottest sports both on screen and off. And one new sport bursting onto the global scene is bossaball. **Bossaball, originating in 2004, is the newest competitive team sport in the world** – and its high-flying blend of volleyball, soccer and gymnastics is capturing attention everywhere from Europe to Asia.

## My Background Evaluating Cutting-Edge Games

As a gaming content creator for over a decade, I’ve built a reputation for identifying rising stars in the interactive entertainment world – whether eSports, live-action roleplaying games or inventive new physical sports that leverage technology. I evaluate these sports’ mass appeal, global growth potential and possible Olympic candidacy.

Bossaball demonstrates tremendous promise in all facets. The visionary concept of Filip Eyckmans, bossaball strategically merges the explosive pace of volleyball with nimble footwork inspired by soccer and jaw-dropping acrobatics akin to gymnasts. This intersection of established sports played upon a bouncy court featuring trampolines on either side of the net creates sheer spectacle. The athleticism required to strike a ball mid-air while coordinating team formations introduces skilful complexity absent from most traditional sports.

## Bossaball Court Set-Up and Rule Highlights

Bossaball is contested between two teams of 4 or 5 players on a 10 by 20 meter inflatable court. Users may employ hands, feet or head – as in soccer‘s heading – to pass and strike the ball.

*   Teams alternate contacts with the ball across the net, up to 3 touches allowed per possession
*   Players jump from trampolines integrated along each sideline for gravity-defying spikes, blocks and digs 
*   Controlled net contact expands volley exchanges not seen in volleyball
*   Up to two player substitutions per team per set 

Matches consist of best 3-out-of-5 sets rally scored to 25 points, winning by a two point margin. Bossaball sessions also uniquely integrate music and lighting effects to punctuate epic rallies, further energizing the crowd.

## Recent Bossaball Growth Statistics

While originally founded in Belgium, bossaball‘s headquarters shifted to Barcelona, Spain given passionate European adoption. As of 2023:

*   **450+ bossaball courts** across **47 countries** worldwide and 6 continents
*   Approximtely **8-10 new countries** add bossaball courts annually 
*   Brazil, Spain, France and Slovakia home to most thriving national pro leagues 
*   **35% participation growth in North America** from 2021 to 2022
*   2024 debut as **demonstration sport at Asia Games** and 2028 **Central American/Caribbean Games**

## Projecting Bossaball‘s Future Appeal

While alternatives like spikeball and bubble soccer gain momentary notoriety, both lack bossaball‘s creative foundations in popular sports to enable sustained mainstream appeal. Volleyball and soccer aficionados will recognize familiar gameplay elements while dazzling aerial acrobatics attract wider entertainment seekers.

As international growth rates demonstrate, I project bossaball cementing itself alongside established games like rugby or lacrosse over the next decade. Innovative adoption as a demonstration event in leading competitions like the Asia Games foreshadows full medal status. And bossaball’s accessibility regardless of age, gender or body type strengthens its case as an Olympic dark horse candidate.

Given relentless digital immersion today, spectator sports guaranteeing live thrills will only increase in value – and bossaball promises those in spades. Its vibrant merging of team dynamics, live music and physics-defying stunts make bossaball set to become _the_ trending sport for 2025 and beyond!

# A brief history of the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup

29 January, 2026

[](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.icc-cricket.com%2Fmedia-releases%2Fa-brief-history-of-the-icc-men-s-t20-world-cup)[](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.icc-cricket.com%2Fmedia-releases%2Fa-brief-history-of-the-icc-men-s-t20-world-cup&text=A%20brief%20history%20of%20the%20ICC%20Men%E2%80%99s%20T20%20World%20Cup)

![Image 18: Carlos Brathwaite 'Remember the Moment' Six | Bira Six Days of Sixes](https://images.icc-cricket.com/image/upload/t_ratio16_9-size30-webp/prd/ovelcptcripw8cqf09nq)

**Media release**

We are now nearly two decades removed from the introduction of the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup, which ushered in a new era for the game when India emerged victorious from that thrilling 2007 tournament in South Africa.

There were 12 teams competing in that inaugural outing, while there will be 20 teams from all corners of the globe competing to win the tournament’s 10th edition in 2026. Six different teams have lifted the trophy over the years, with the West Indies, England and reigning champions India the only nations to have won it twice.

Ahead of the 2026 tournament in India and Sri Lanka, let’s take a little trip down memory lane.

**A new form of cricket**

The 21st century has stood witness to the emergence of T20 cricket as one of sport’s fastest growing formats, but there was major scepticism when it was first mooted around English county cricket circles.

Initially seen as a way to attract new people to the sport and simplify the game to wider audiences, T20 cricket has transformed the game’s landscape since first being introduced at the professional level in 2003 and then quickly adopted around the world.

The birth of the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup in 2007 took it to another level and that tournament’s impact was immediate.

Legendary West Indian Chris Gayle was responsible for that, sending the very first ball of the tournament to the fence before smashing a remarkable 117 against the hosts – making the first ever T20I century in the process.

From bowl-outs to Yuvraj Singh taking six sixes off one Stuart Broad over and Misbah-ul-Haq’s infamous scoop in the final, that first tournament proved an historic first edition.

Culminating in India’s stunning victory over Pakistan, it not only set a new course for the modern game but also the tone for the drama that would follow at ICC Men’s T20 World Cups in the decades to follow.

**Iconic moments**

Pakistan avenged their loss to India by claiming victory in 2009, as Shahid Afridi, a player born for the format, shone with both bat and ball in England. The tournament also saw the hosts stunned by the Netherlands in one of the all-time great upsets.

England responded a year later in the Caribbean by winning their first men’s white-ball trophy as Kevin Pietersen earned Player of the Tournament honours for his efforts with the bat.

Then in 2012, West Indies joined the party by triumphing in Sri Lanka, with Marlon Samuels (78) and Sunil Narine (3-9) the stars of the show in the final.

They beat the hosts to lift the trophy that year, but Sri Lanka bounced back by winning in 2014 to ensure Kumar Sangakkara and Mahela Jayawardene bowed out of the format in style.

The West Indies were back on top of the world two years later thanks to Carlos Brathwaite’s four consecutive sixes off Ben Stokes in the last over of the 2016 final in Kolkota, a moment etched in cricket’s collective memory thanks Ian Bishop’s immortal “remember the name” call on commentary.

After a five-year absence, the ICC Men’s T20 World Cup resumed in 2021 as Australia claimed their first title. David Warner and Mitchell Marsh were the heroes in the final against New Zealand.

A year later, it was England who triumphed for a second time, ensuring they held both the T20 and ODI world titles. Sam Curran stole the show that year and was both named Player of the Match in the final and Player of the Tournament for his all-round contributions.

**Going global**

In 2024, the tournament expanded from 16 teams to 20, with the USA, Canada and Uganda making their debuts.

The Americans, co-hosting alongside the West Indies, seized their opportunity with a stunning Super Over victory over Pakistan as they progressed to the Super 8 stage. Afghanistan also enjoyed a dream run, making it to the semi-finals of a major ICC tournament for the first time.

Virat Kohli saved his best for last in the final with 76, but that did not look like it would be enough until a magical spell from Jasprit Bumrah derailed South Africa’s chase and set up an seven-run victory for India.

As with Sangakkara and Jayawardene a decade earlier, this proved to be a final farewell for two modern greats as Kohli and Rohit Sharma both called time on their international T20 careers.

That means new faces in 2026, and another new team in Italy, who will look to hit the ground running when they make their World Cup debut in India and Sri Lanka.

The **Super League World Nines** (known as the _[Gatorade](link_6) Super League World Nines_ due to sponsorship), was a pre-season [rugby league nines](link_7) tournament between national sides. Set up in the midst of the [Super League war](link_8) and created in opposition to the [Australian Rugby League](link_9)'s [World Sevens](link_10) tournament, the tournament was held twice before being abandoned when the two factions merged to form the [National Rugby League](link_11).

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Super_League_World_Nines&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 1996 Super League World Nines Tournament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Super_League_World_Nines&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1996  Super League World Nines Tournament")]

The 1996 World Nines were held at [National Stadium](link_12) in [Suva](link_13), [Fiji](link_14) from 22 February to 24 February. The winner of this competition was [New Zealand](link_5), who won their first world trophy in a [rugby league](link_3) competition.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_World_Nines#cite_note-nzrl48-1) New Zealand were awarded A$30,000 for the win.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_World_Nines#cite_note-scots-2)

The 1996 World Nines marked the first time that a video referee was used for a game of Rugby League or Rugby Union . Due to a court ruling in the [Federal Court of Australia](link_15), this was the only Super League competition held in 1996.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_World_Nines#cite_note-chris-3)

### 1997 Tournament

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Super_League_World_Nines&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1997 Tournament")]

The 1997 World Nines were held in [Townsville, Queensland](link_16) from 31 January to 2 February. New Zealand won this competition for the second year in a row.

## Squads

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Super_League_World_Nines&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Squads")]

### 1996 Tournament.

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Super_League_World_Nines&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1996 Tournament.")]

All teams were selected as professional playing squads.

Sixteen squads competed in Suva:[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_World_Nines#cite_note-scots-2) - Ireland played in a warm up test V's Australia at the Fiji National Stadium in the week leading up to the World Nines. 14 February 1996. Australia winning 22:12.

John Kirwan (New Zealand) won a Rugby Union World Cup Winners Medal with the All Blacks in the 1st ever Rugby World Cup 1987. Kirwan would go on to Coach both Italy and Japan National Rugby Union Teams

Henry Paul (New Zealand) would represent ~ Bath, Gloucester and England in Rugby Union.

[Gary Connolly](link_17), of England, and [Martin Hall](link_18), the Welsh captain, were forced to withdraw from their respective squads after being threatened with legal action by the [Australian Rugby League](link_9).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_World_Nines#cite_note-4)

*Gary Connolly would go on to transfer to play for Munster Rugby Union 1998 - Ireland.

Scott Quinnell, Allan Bateman (Wales) would both return to Rugby Union and play for the British & Irish Lions in the winning series v's South Africa.

Iestyn Harris (Wales) would represent Wales in Rugby Union.

Andy Farrell (England) went on the represent England in Rugby Union, and to coach England and later Ireland in Rugby Union

Georgie Graham (Scotland) would represent Scotland in Rugby Union

NEW ZEALAND

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Defunct rugby league sevens tournament

World Sevens[![Image 6](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/1/1e/Rugby_league_world_sevens_logo.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rugby_league_world_sevens_logo.gif)
Sport[Rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league")
Instituted 1988
Ceased 2004
Region International
Holders[Wests Tigers](link_3)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-stewartrleague1-1) (2004)
Most titles[Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles](link_4) (3 titles)

The **Rugby League World Sevens**, usually referred to as the **World Sevens**[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-BBC-02-02-03-2) and sometimes as the **World Cup Sevens**,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3) was a pre-season [rugby league sevens](link_5) tournament made up over the years primarily of [New South Wales Rugby League](link_6) (NSWRL), [Australian Rugby League](link_7) (ARL) and mostly recently [National Rugby League](link_8) (NRL) teams, along with teams representing NSW Country and nations including Tonga, France, Papua New Guinea, Samoa, Russia, Fiji, the US and England.

When the [National Rugby League](link_8) was formed in Australasia in 1998 the World Sevens competition was dropped, but it returned in 2003 when Parramatta successfully defended their title from the last time in 1997.

## Format and rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_League_World_Sevens&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Format and rules")]

The World Sevens format saw entrants divided into eight pools.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3) The top team in each pool progressed into the quarter-finals.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3)

Until 2004, second placed teams from each pool would play each other, as would third placed teams. In 2004, when the competition was known as the _Cougar Bourbon World Sevens_, this format changed, when only the top placed teams played for the major prize.

Each match played up to and including the semi-finals had two 7-minute halves with extra time played in the event of tie at the end normal time.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3) The final is longer with two 10-minute halves. In 2004, the tackle limit was reduced from 6 to 4.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_League_World_Sevens&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

The World Sevens were held at [Parramatta Stadium](link_9) from 1988 to 1991 and [Sydney Football Stadium](link_10) from 1992 to 2004, with the 1995 tournament's opening day being held at [Suncorp Stadium](link_11) in Brisbane, and the 1996 tournament's opening day taking place at [Parramatta Stadium](link_9).

[Wigan](link_12) played in the rain-soaked 1992 World Sevens as they opted to fulfil a promise made by their club's chairman, [Maurice Lindsay](link_13), to appear despite having commitments in the [Challenge Cup](link_14).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3) After a win in extra time against [Cronulla](link_15) in the opening match hinted at a strong challenge for the title, a poor performance and loss to the [Gold Coast Seagulls](link_16) saw Wigan's challenge seeming likely to fail.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3) The group stage ended with each team in Wigan's group having won one game, but by virtue of "most tries scored" they proceeded to the quarter-finals, despite their chances being largely written off.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3)[John Monie](link_17), the Wigan coach, told his team, "We've copped a bit of a bagging in the press today saying we're a typical Pommy side and can't tackle ... and the other thing was that they say 'Oh, [Penrith](link_18)'s got the easy draw again because they're playing Wigan'".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3) In the event, Wigan breezed past Penrith 22–8 in the quarter-final and a [Denis Betts](link_19) try in extra time won the semi-final against Manly. Scorer of six tries before the game, [Martin Offiah](link_20), the Man of the Series, scored four more in the final played against the [Brisbane Broncos](link_21) (the former club of Wigan's new recruit for 1992, [Gene Miles](link_22)), a game Wigan won 18–6.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-3)

1993 saw Wigan not defending their title. [Eastern Suburbs](link_23) defeated [Manly Warringah](link_24) in the final. The Sea Eagles would go on to win both the 1994 and 1995 World Sevens defeating [St George](link_25) and [Fiji](link_26) respectively. Manly's wins actually could have been potentially embarrassing for the tournaments organisers. During these two years the Sevens major sponsor was [Coca-Cola](link_27) who put up the [A$](link_28)100,000 winners purse. At the time of their wins, Manly Warringah's major sponsor was Coke's major rival [Pepsi](link_29).

In 1996, [Canada](link_30) became the first side in World Sevens not to score a point throughout the tournament. The Canadians lost to the [Newcastle Knights](link_31) 52–0 and [New Zealand](link_32) 56–0 in the group stage and to [Western Suburbs](link_33) 48–0 in the plate quarter-finals.

[Nathan Hindmarsh](link_34) was deemed Player of the Series as [Parramatta](link_35) stormed to victory in the 2003 competition. Parramatta beat [Canberra](link_36) in their quarter-final, followed by [South Sydney](link_37) in the semi-final.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-BBC-02-02-03-2) The final pitted [England](link_38) against a Parramatta side that flew to the lead, scoring five tries before half-time to England's one by [Keith Senior](link_39).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-BBC-02-02-03-2) The match finished 42–18.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-BBC-02-02-03-2) The Plate final was won by the [Bulldogs](link_40) who beat New Zealand and the Bowl final was won by [North Queensland](link_41) who beat [Fiji](link_26).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-BBC-02-02-03-2)

In 2004, the [Wests Tigers](link_3) took the title, winning 18–7 in the final and ending Parramatta's campaign for a third consecutive title.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-stewartrleague1-1) The Wests Tigers' first title as a merged entity gained them A$100,000 in prize money.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens#cite_note-stewartrleague1-1)

### 2004: tournament ceases

**Rugby league football**, commonly known as **rugby league,** is a [full-contact sport](link_16) played by two teams of thirteen players on a rectangular [field](link_15) measuring 68 m (74 yd) wide and 112–122 m (122–133 yd) long with H-shaped posts at both ends.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league#cite_note-pitch_and_post_dimensions-1) It is one of the [two major codes](link_17) of [rugby football](link_18), the other being [rugby union](link_4).[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league#cite_note-3)

It originated in 1895 in [Huddersfield](link_19), West Yorkshire, England, as the result of a [split](link_10) from the [Rugby Football Union](link_20) (RFU) over the issue of payments to players.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league#cite_note-Tony_Collins_2006_p.3-4) The rules of the game governed by the new [Northern Rugby Football Union](link_21) progressively changed from those of the RFU with the specific aim of producing a faster and more entertaining game to appeal to paying spectators, on whose income the new organisation and its members depended.

In rugby league, points are scored by carrying an oval [ball](link_22) and touching it to the ground beyond the opposing team's goal line; this is called a _[try](link_23)_, and is the primary method of scoring, worth four points. The opposing team attempts to stop the attacking side scoring points by [tackling](link_24) the player carrying the ball and denying forward progress. On occasion, where a clear try scoring opportunity has been thwarted by foul play, a penalty try may be awarded without the ball being grounded over the try line. In addition to tries, points can be scored by kicking goals. [Drop goals](link_25) (or field goals) can be attempted from the hand at any time for a single point. 9-a-side version of rugby league

**Rugby league nines** (or simply **nines**) is a version of [rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league") football played with nine players on each side. The game is substantially the same as full rugby league, with some differences in [rules](link_9) and shorter games. Nines is usually played in festivals, as its shorter game play allows for a tournament to be completed in a day or over a single weekend.

In July 2021, [International Rugby League](link_4) (IRL) chair [Troy Grant](link_10) stated that the organisation was considering a bid for rugby league nines to be played at the [2032 Summer Olympics](link_11) in Brisbane. [Rugby sevens](link_12), a similarly-condensed version of [rugby union](link_13), has been a core Olympic event since [2016](link_14).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines#cite_note-1)

## Laws

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_nines&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Laws")]

The laws of the game are the same as [standard rugby league laws](link_9) with the following exceptions.

*   Each team is allowed a squad of up to fifteen players, with no more than nine players on the field at any time. Unlimited substitutions are allowed from a named bench of four players.
*   The match lasts for 18 minutes, divided into two halves of 9 minutes. There is no half time interval but teams are allowed a maximum of 1 minute to change ends. Each half starts with a place kick.
*   Scrums consist of no more than 5 forwards, with a maximum 3 in the front row and 2 in the second row. When the ball is in the scrum no more than 4 players from each team shall act as backs. The ball must emerge from behind the feet of the second row.
*   Conversions after a successful try take the form of drop kicks. Players from the team that has conceded the score do not have to retire behind the try line but must not interfere with any conversion attempt.
*   When points have been scored the team against which points have been scored will restart the game with a tap restart from the centre of the half-way line.
*   When a team is awarded a penalty then play must proceed by way of a tap 10-metres in advance of where the infringement took place.
*   In the event of misconduct by a player the referee can suspend for 5 minutes. In the [Carnegie Floodlit Nines](link_15), a major nines competition, this has been reduced to 2 minutes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines#cite_note-SL14906-04-08-09-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Version of rugby league football

This article is about the sport derived from [rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"); not to be confused with [Rugby sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_sevens "Rugby sevens").

Rugby league sevens| Highest [governing body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_governing_body "Sports governing body") | [Rugby League International Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_International_Federation "Rugby League International Federation") |
| --- |
| First played | 1961, Australia |
| Characteristics |
| Contact | [Full](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contact_sport#Full-contact "Contact sport") |
| Team members | 12 (7 on field + 5 interchange) |
| [Mixed-sex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-sex_sports "Mixed-sex sports") | Single |
| Type | Outdoor |
| Equipment | [Football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_(ball)#Rugby_football "Football (ball)") |
| Venue | [Rugby league playing field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_playing_field "Rugby league playing field") |

**Rugby league sevens** (or simply **sevens**) is a seven-a-side derivative of [rugby league football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"), which is usually a thirteen-a-side sport. The game is substantially the same as full [rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"), with some rule changes and shorter games. Sevens is usually played in festivals, as its shorter game play allows for a tournament to be completed in a day or over a single weekend.

As well as being played by club sides, rugby league sevens is particularly popular with social teams, formed in the workplace or from the patrons of a public house for example, as it is often difficult in these places to form a full squad of 13 players and four substitutes of regular players. Some tournaments prefer to play [rugby league nines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines "Rugby league nines") (rugby league with nine players on each side) to distinguish it from [rugby union sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union_sevens "Rugby union sevens").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The game of [rugby sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_sevens "Rugby sevens") dates back to its invention by [Ned Haig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Haig "Ned Haig") in [Melrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melrose,_Scotland "Melrose, Scotland") in the [Scottish Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Borders "Scottish Borders") in 1883, just over a decade before the schism in [rugby football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") in 1895, which led to the creation of rugby league and [rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union"). However, rugby sevens did not spread outside Scotland before the 1920s. That said, the larger part of Scotland's rugby league players have come from Borders backgrounds.

The record rugby league sevens attendance remains the 80,000 that attended a 1933 match between Australia and England at Roundhay Park in Leeds. This match was also attended by English royalty.

The first rugby _league_ sevens tournament was played in Australia in 1961.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-centofrl1-1)

The major tournament was the [World Sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens "Rugby League World Sevens") played prior to the beginning of the [National Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League "National Rugby League") season in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), Australia. That tournament has been suspended but sevens is played around the world at different levels from junior teams to international ones. Sevens is considered to be a good tool to increase the skills of players and to help emerging rugby league nations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-nrlnewsking1-2)

## Playing area

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Playing area")]

Sevens is played on a standard [rugby league playing field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_playing_field "Rugby league playing field") as defined in Section 1 of the _International Laws of the Game_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-ILG-3)

## Teams

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Teams")]

Teams are composed of three forwards, one half and three backs.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4)

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rules")]

Sevens follows the [rules of 13-a-side rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_of_rugby_league "Laws of rugby league") with exceptions. Each rugby league nation is at liberty to adopt a modified version of international rugby league rules for their own domestic competitions; as a result the rules of rugby league sevens can vary too, even before changes implemented by competition organisers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-rl1908rulesvary-5)

Matches have two halves of seven minutes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4) Unlimited substitutions are allowed from a squad totalling 12 players.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4) In sevens, smaller [scrums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrum_(rugby) "Scrum (rugby)"), formed from the three forwards on each team, are formed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4) All kicks for goal should be [drop kicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drop_kick "Drop kick") in sevens.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4) After points have been scored a tap kick restart is taken by the non-scoring side.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4)

The [World Sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens "Rugby League World Sevens"), the world's premier sevens event while it operated, had two 7 minute halves up to and including the semi-finals with extra time played in the event of tie at the end normal time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-6) The final was longer with two 10-minute halves. In 2004, the World Sevens tackle limit was reduced from 6 to 4.

## Major sevens festivals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Major sevens festivals")]

*   World Sevens was suspended in 2005 because NRL teams were reluctant to field their star players, resulting in dwindling spectator numbers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-nrlnewsking1-2)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unlimgsteven1-7) Play resumed
*   Actor [Russell Crowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Crowe "Russell Crowe") hosts the [Orara Valley Axemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orara_Valley_Axemen "Orara Valley Axemen") Sevens Tournament at Coffs Harbour on the New South Wales North Coast.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unlimgsteven1-7) This tournament is participated in by teams representing countries of the world, local clubs and a few clubs from Brisbane, Australia. In 2005 the [Souths Logan Magpies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Souths_Logan_Magpies "Souths Logan Magpies") from the [Queensland Wizard Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Cup "Queensland Cup") and the [Gold Coast Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_Titans "Gold Coast Titans"), who entered the [NRL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League "National Rugby League") in 2007, were two well known clubs that participated.
*   [Latino Rugby League Sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_Rugby_League_Sevens "Latino Rugby League Sevens")

The **NRL Nines** is a [rugby league nines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines "Rugby league nines") competition, normally held during the [NRL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL "NRL") preseason each year. It was initially held in [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland"), [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), between 2014 and 2017 before going on hiatus.

Returning in 2020, hosting duties moved to [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth"), [Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Australia "Western Australia"), before being cancelled in 2021. The series has not returned since.

## Competition format

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Competition format")]

### Auckland (2014–2017)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Auckland (2014–2017)")]

Two national women's teams compete in one section of the tournament and sixteen NRL club men's teams compete in the other. Each of the men's squad must include at least 12 of their top 25 players in their squad, and at least one marquee player. The winner of the men's tournament received [AUD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUD "AUD")$500,000 with a total prize pool of AUD$2,250,000. In the first four editions, the competition has had eight different finalists and four different winners, though the 2016 title was later stripped from the Parramatta Eels for breaching the salary cap.

Since 2015 the [Kiwiferns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_women's_national_rugby_league_team "New Zealand women's national rugby league team") and the [Jillaroos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_women's_national_rugby_league_team "Australia women's national rugby league team") also competed in a three-game series, with the Kiwiferns winning the series 2-1. These games are played during the final stages of the men's tournament and allow the male players more of a break between their games while providing a broader tournament. Also in 2015, the pools were given traditional Maori names that were chosen by a public vote and were: [Rangitoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangitoto "Rangitoto"), [Waiheke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiheke "Waiheke"), [Piha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piha "Piha") and [Hunua Ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunua_Ranges "Hunua Ranges").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-2)

### Perth (2020)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Perth (2020)")]

The women's teams were [NRL Women's Premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Women's_Premiership "NRL Women's Premiership") sides instead of national teams.

### Series Cancellations (2021–2024)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Series Cancellations (2021–2024)")]

The 2021 series was cancelled entirely, not due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Australia "COVID-19 pandemic in Australia"), but due to an overly-crowded preseason schedule.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-4)

When the 2022 Fixtures list was released by the NRL, it included no mention of the [World Club Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Club_Challenge "World Club Challenge") or NRL Nines competitions.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-5)

The [World Club Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Club_Challenge "World Club Challenge") did make its return in 2023, and again in 2024, but the NRL Nines competition was absent for both years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-6)

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Rules")]

There are a number of rule variations that are implemented to ensure the games are faster and to ensure fewer delays and stoppages.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-7)

The major rule changes that differ from regular NRL games are:

*   Two nine-minute halves with a two-minute half time period.
*   Nine players a side with five unlimited interchange players (six interchanges in 2014).
*   Scrums are only formed after a double knock on, with attacking teams electing which side to feed the ball.
*   No video referee, with one on-field referee, two touch judges and two in-goal judges.
*   Five minute golden try period in qualifying rounds with the match deemed a draw if there is no score, while unlimited golden try for the finals.
*   A tap restart takes place after a 40/20.
*   Five points for a try scored in the bonus zone under the posts, with two point drop kick conversion attempts.
*   The scoring team will have a drop-kick kick-off at the half way mark to restart play.
*   Three minute sin bins (Five in 2014).
*   Five tackles in a set.

## Finals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Finals")]

**Note** – The [Parramatta Eels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parramatta_Eels "Parramatta Eels") were stripped of their 2016 Auckland Nines title due to a breach of the [NRL salary cap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_salary_cap "NRL salary cap"). From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Manningham_fc_1896_team.jpg/250px-Manningham_fc_1896_team.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Manningham_fc_1896_team.jpg)

The [Manningham F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manningham_F.C. "Manningham F.C.") team that won the [1895–96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1895%E2%80%9396_Northern_Rugby_Football_Union_season "1895–96 Northern Rugby Football Union season") championship, posing with the shield awarded.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rugby_league#cite_note-1) The club was the first rugby league champion of the [Northern RFU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_League "Rugby Football League") and the first in the world. After a series of meetings in 1903 the club committee decided to leave the rugby code and switch to [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rugby_league#cite_note-f11-2) becoming current [Bradford City A.F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford_City_A.F.C. "Bradford City A.F.C.")

The **history of rugby league** as a separate form of [rugby football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") goes back to 1895 in [Huddersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huddersfield "Huddersfield"), [West Riding of Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Riding_of_Yorkshire "West Riding of Yorkshire") when the [Northern Rugby Football Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_League "Rugby Football League") broke away from England's established [Rugby Football Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union") to administer its own separate competition.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rugby_league#cite_note-begin-3) Similar schisms occurred later in Australia and New Zealand in 1907. Gradually the rugby played in these breakaway competitions evolved into a distinctly separate sport that took its name from the professional leagues that administered it. [Rugby league in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_in_England "Rugby league in England") went on to set attendance and player payment records and [rugby league in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_in_Australia "Rugby league in Australia") became the second most watched sport on television. The game also developed a significant place in the culture of [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_in_France "Rugby league in France"), [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_in_New_Zealand "Rugby league in New Zealand") and several other Pacific Island nations, such as [Papua New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_in_Papua_New_Guinea "Rugby league in Papua New Guinea"), where it has become the national sport.

## Rugby before the schisms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_rugby_league&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Rugby before the schisms")]

Further information: [History of rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rugby_union "History of rugby union")

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Rochdale_hornets_1875.jpg/250px-Rochdale_hornets_1875.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rochdale_hornets_1875.jpg)

[Rochdale Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale_Hornets "Rochdale Hornets") team of 1875, one of the early rugby football clubs that then switched to rugby league

Although many forms of football had been played across the world, it was only during the second half of the 19th century that these games began to be codified. In 1871, English clubs playing the version of football played at [Rugby School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_School "Rugby School"), which involved much more handling of the ball than in association football, met to form the [Rugby Football Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union"). Many new rugby clubs were formed, and it was in the [Northern English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_England "Northern England")[counties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County "County") of [Lancashire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancashire "Lancashire") and [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire") that the game really took hold. Here rugby was largely a working class game, whilst the south eastern clubs were largely middle class.

Rugby spread to [Australasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia "Australasia"), especially the cities of [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), [Brisbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane "Brisbane"), [Christchurch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christchurch "Christchurch") and [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland"). Here too there was a clear divide between the working and more affluent upper-class players.

The strength of support for rugby grew over the following years, and large paying crowds were attracted to major matches, in particular in Yorkshire, where matches in the [Yorkshire Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire_Cup_(rugby_union) "Yorkshire Cup (rugby union)") (_T'owd Tin Pot_) soon became major events. England teams of the era were dominated by Lancashire and Yorkshire players. However these players were forbidden to earn any of the spoils of this newly-rich game. Predominantly working class teams found it difficult to play to their full potential because in many cases their time to play and to train was limited by the need to earn a wage. A further limit on the playing ability of working class teams was that working class players had to be careful how hard they played. If injured, they had to pay their own medical bills and possibly take time off work, which for a man earning a weekly wage could easily lead to financial hardship.

## The schism and the birth of rugby league

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=History_of_rugby_league&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: The schism and the birth of rugby league")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/Reverend_marshall.jpg/250px-Reverend_marshall.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Reverend_marshall.jpg)

A cartoon lampooning the divide in rugby. The caricatures are of Rev. Frank Marshall, an arch-opponent of broken-time payments and James Miller, a long-time opponent of Marshall

In 1892, charges of professionalism were laid against [rugby football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") clubs in [Bradford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford "Bradford") and [Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds "Leeds"), both in [Yorkshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yorkshire "Yorkshire"), after they compensated players for missing work. This was despite the fact that the English [Rugby Football Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union") (RFU) was allowing other players to be paid, such as the [1888 British Isles team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1888_British_Lions_tour_to_New_Zealand_and_Australia "1888 British Lions tour to New Zealand and Australia") that toured Australia, or the account of [Harry Hamill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Hamill "Harry Hamill") of his payments to represent [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_Waratahs "New South Wales Waratahs") (NSW) against [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_rugby_union_team "England national rugby union team") in 1904.[_[relevant?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Writing\_better\_articles#Stay\_on\_topic "Wikipedia:Writing better articles")_][_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1893 Yorkshire clubs complained that southern clubs were over-represented on the RFU committee and that committee meetings were held in London at times that made it difficult for northern members to attend. By implication they were arguing that this affected the RFU's decisions on the issue of "broken time" payments (as compensation for the loss of income) to the detriment of northern clubs, who made up the majority of English rugby clubs. Payment for broken time was a proposal put forward by Yorkshire clubs that would allow players to receive up to six shillings  (equivalent to £33 in present-day terms)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rugby_league#cite_note-inflation-UK-4) when they missed work because of match commitments. The idea was voted down by the RFU.

In August 1893, Huddersfield signed star players George Boak and John 'Jock' Forsyth from Carlisle-based club, Cummersdale Hornets.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rugby_league#cite_note-5) The transfer was sudden and both men were summoned to appear before Carlisle Magistrates' Court for leaving their jobs without giving proper notice.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rugby_league#cite_note-6) Huddersfield was also accused of offering cash inducements for the players to move clubs contrary to the strict rules of the RFU. After an investigation, Huddersfield eventually received a long suspension from playing matches.

The severity of the punishments for "broken time" payments and their widespread application to northern clubs and players contributed to a growing sense of frustration and absence of fair play. Meanwhile, there was an obvious comparison with the professional [Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Football_League "The Football League") which had been formed in 1888, comprising 12 association football clubs, six of whom were from [Northern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_England "Northern England"). In this environment, the next logical step was for the northern rugby clubs to form their own professional league.

On 27 August 1895, as a result of an emergency meeting in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), prominent Lancashire clubs [Broughton Rangers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broughton_Rangers "Broughton Rangers"), [Leigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leigh_Centurions "Leigh Centurions"), [Oldham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldham_R.L.F.C. "Oldham R.L.F.C."), [Rochdale Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochdale_Hornets "Rochdale Hornets"), [St. Helens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Helens_R.F.C. "St Helens R.F.C."), [Tyldesley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyldesley_FC "Tyldesley FC"), [Warrington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warrington_Wolves "Warrington Wolves"), [Widnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Widnes_Vikings "Widnes Vikings") and [Wigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigan_Warriors "Wigan Warriors") declared that they would support their Yorkshire colleagues in their proposal to form a Northern Union.

# 'An unbelievable story' - inside unfancied Wakefield's rapid ascent

Figure caption, 

Wakefield are champions for the first time in since 1968 beating Warrington

By Matt Newsum

BBC Sport Rugby League journalist

*   Published 2 October 2026 

Updated 3 October 2026

**There is a moment in the 1939 film 'The Wizard of Oz' where Dorothy swaps her monochrome world for glorious, eye-opening technicolour the minute she touches down in the Land of Oz.**

The same could be said for the moment that Wakefield Trinity got their hands on the Super League trophy when they beat Warrington Wolves 23-10 in Saturday's Grand Final.

Metaphorically of course, but the achievements of that great club had before only been seen in those black and white hues and so were ripe for a dash of colour.

Derek 'Rocky' Turner, Neil Fox MBE, Don Fox, Harold Poynton, Ken Rollin... all legends of the 1960s and an era when all the silverware found its way to WF1.

Belle Vue, or the DIY Kitchens Stadium as it is now known, has had its special nights since, such as the win to relegate rivals Castleford and secure safety at their expense in 2006.

Amid all the adrenaline and excitement, that was survival. Not success.

Yet, this season has followed a different storyline. Wakefield could achieve something. Wakefield could be winners.

And that they are, landing their first title since 1968.

Daryl Powell tapped into the historical significance of the Grand Final in the build up to the showdown, as winger Tom Johnstone explained before the showpiece event.

"Daryl put a Powerpoint presentation on the screen, and said 'You could be legends of this club', and that was it," Johnstone told BBC Radio 5 live just days before scoring a try in the Grand Final and picking up the Rob Burrow Award as man of the match.

"He didn't really go any further into it, he just put a seed in the back of your mind and just gave you that little nugget."

*   [Victory parade celebrates Super League champions](https://www.bbc.com/news/live/cr15j33d53g8t) 

## All change in WF1

![Image 1: Wakefield's Championship winning side of 1967 poses with the trophy in the dressing room while clutching bottles of beer and other alcohol as a celebration](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/57a4/live/7ecd3ec0-bd8b-11f1-b442-f3f672c979ff.jpg)Image source, Getty Images

Image caption, 

The team of the 1960s was the last Wakefield team to enjoy sustained achievement at the top level

Going back to the movie theme, Wakefield's resurrection over the past three seasons is almost too fanciful for Hollywood's scriptwriters, given the rapid ascent.

Owner Matt Ellis is without doubt the lead character, having come in as a fan but also an incredibly wealthy and successful kitchen magnate.

It has been more than just investment thrown at it; for example Ellis has been hands-on with the stadium renovation in terms of standards and finish on the back of the work of former custodians Michael Carter and John Minards who set the ball rolling.

He also has brought drive and vision, and it was he who was determined to bring Powell to the club as head coach almost immediately after taking control.

"Everything has changed from the top to the bottom," Johnstone added. "Rather than going into individual key details, the facilities have changed, the manner of the club, just the belief and the ambition of the club is probably the best one.

"We used to say a lot of things and say we wanted to compete but we had no chance of doing it at the time. Whereas now, it's an elite club. It's run so well.

"Anything you need, you've got it. Matt will provide absolutely anything. He just wants to see success. And the players we've signed and the team we've built, it just shows. It's just night and day."

Ellis and Powell has been a near-perfect partnership; with promotion back to Super League, Wembley success in the 1895 Cup, and back-to-back play-off appearances in Super League all culminating in the glorious win at Old Trafford.

Powell had enjoyed success at Featherstone and Castleford before a stint at Warrington ended prematurely, and joining Wakefield has had a revitalising impact on both club and coach.

"This is an unbelievable story," Powell said.

"From me thinking a bloke's trying to sell me a kitchen to winning the Super League is phenomenal. It's been an unbelievable three years.

"I'm amazed really at the boys and how good they've been. Obviously, it's pretty sweet for me tonight as an individual but for the club, the players, the coaching staff, everything that we've built up over the last three years is phenomenal.

"What happened tonight is the best thing that could have happened to Super League, 100%. A sell-out crowd and a team like us, you know the story before the game, it's awesome. It shows the [salary] cap is working as a team like us can come from the Championship and win in two years, that's big."

[Wakefield beat Warrington to win Super League](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-league/articles/c39w4w7pzqv4o)

    

    *   Published 1 day ago 

*   [Super League Grand Final as it happened: Wakefield beat Warrington to win first Super League title](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-league/live/c8046w559k6zt) 

## Family feel and a tight bond

![Image 2: Caius Faatili (centre) in action for Wakefield against Warrington in the Super League Grand Final](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2048/cpsprodpb/5457/live/016e0010-bf6e-11f1-8353-af47de35c0c8.jpg)Image source, PA Media

Image caption, 

Caius Faatili, known as 'Captain Chaos' at Wakefield, is an eyecatching figure with his aggressive, all-energy style

Powell has turned to familiar faces to fill those key roles; Michael Shenton - once his captain at Castleford, is now his trusted assistant while Ste Mills - another acolyte of yore is the brains behind the recruitment.

Aside from that, former Trinity player and modern day favourite Danny Kirmond is also on the staff while the experienced Stu Dickens also adds to the brains trust.

On the pitch, Powell has reunited with Jake Trueman, whose form in his time at Castleford put him in the international picture, and Mike McMeeken, who was part of the 2017 team at the Tigers who lost to Leeds in the Grand Final.

Front-rower McMeeken's authority and presence were a huge pick up for Trinity when he signed from Catalans as a statement signing on their top flight return, part of a powerful pack which highlights the best of Mills' talentspotting.

Bringing that power are Ky Rodwell from NRL side Parramatta, and ex-Cronulla reserve grader Caleb Hamlin-Uele - both signed while Trinity were still in the Championship.

Since getting up, Caius Faatili was brought in from Queensland Cup side Sunshine Coast Falcons in 2025 and was an immediate success with his raw-boned and aggressive style; lean, muscular Isaiah Vagana is rangy and athletic in the back-row, while Samoa international Jazz Tevaga has brought NRL experience and abrasive swagger to the squad.

"Daryl's really shown how good of a coach he is just how he's brought players in that probably may not have been picked up because of not being as well known," McMeeken told BBC Sport.

"For example Caius, not many clubs would have known about him but he's seen the potential in him and the good thing is, I think he's only about 23 or 24 so it's quite scary to see how far people like him can actually go."

*   
[Quiz: Name every Super League Grand Finalist](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-league/articles/cmp8d6dknk07o)

    

    *   Published 3 days ago 

## 'It still doesn't feel real'

![Image 3: Tom Johnstone slams down a try for Wakefield in their Super League Grand Final win over Warrington](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/c451/live/51ba55f0-bf6e-11f1-8353-af47de35c0c8.jpg)Image source, PA Media

Image caption, 

Tom Johnstone started his professional career with Wakefield and has had two spells culminating in 124 tries in 163 games

Without a major football club in the city, Wakefield Trinity are the prime attraction for support, and all the attention and focus has been shone on them this week.

More than 30,000 tickets were sold for Old Trafford at Trinity's end, nudging the attendance past 71,000 for the sold-out showpiece that guaranteed a new name on the trophy for the second year running.

Finishing fourth earned them a home eliminator where Leigh were beaten impressively, but it was the dismantling of treble-chasing Wigan in the semi-final which really caught the eye and gave growing hope that Trinity could create a seismic Super League shock.

The Wakefield club that Johnstone started out at is almost a different beast more than a decade on, for the better, but the fanbase has remained the same - committed, loyal and vocal.

"It can only be good for rugby league and Super League for us to be growing and performing and it's finally pay back for all the loyal fans that have been here throughout the years," he said.

After the victory, captain McMeeken said he found himself lost in the ecstasy of the moment and joy of the club's long suffering supporters.

"I don't know when this will sink in. It still doesn't feel real now," he said.

"Even when the final hooter went, just looking at the crowd and seeing the jubilation in all the guys. Maybe tomorrow when we do the parade, it might start to sink in.

"I'm just unbelievably proud of the boys and what we can give back to the city. The tough times they've been through in terms of supporting the club when it was at its lowest and still being loyal and two years later being able to lift that trophy in front of them, that was pretty special."

It is a long time between drinks, 1968. But after 58 years Wakefield have got to sip champagne after the final hooter in Manchester.

Wakefield are back, and the key for everyone at the club now is to ensure they stay there.

Saturday's triumph could be the catalyst for that. Wakefield - Wizards of Old Trafford has a ring to it, or Wizards of OT you might say.
