# Salty celebrations, questionable signings and Test bolters - Prem talking points

![Image 1: George Furbank, Louis Rees Zammit and Charlie Atkinson in a composite images](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/e110/live/a03853f0-c0ac-11f1-bc2e-018d645d8d21.png)Image source, Getty Images

Image caption, 

Only three teams - Gloucester, Bristol and Bath - have won both their games after the opening two rounds of the Prem

By

[Mike Henson](https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/topics/c8ep7j8w1xkt)

BBC Sport rugby union news reporter

*   Published 1 hour ago 

**The stats piled up after a car-crash performance by Harlequins**[**in a 48-0 shellacking by Gloucester.**](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/cw305gm8j591o)

The biggest league defeat in 26 years. Seventeen penalties conceded. Only two entries made into the opposition 22m. Not one of their starting forward pack making more than four carries.

It was a desperately under-powered display.

Boss Jason Gilmore described it as "totally unacceptable" in the aftermath.

The Australian has overseen a few eyesores during his time in charge; a 38-0 reverse at Sandy Park and a 40-14 reverse at the club's festive fixture at Allianz Stadium come to mind.

Gilmore says turning around the tanker will take time. Contracts have to run down and money reassigned to different areas of the squad.

Full-back George Furbank was this summer's big investment. The 29-year-old marked his Prem debut for his new club with a couple of trademark breaks, slicing up from backfield.

He is a classy addition, but is he the signing they needed, with little room to manoeuvre under the salary cap and a creaking forward pack limiting the supply of ball to the backline?

England loosehead prop Fin Baxter has been out for 10 months with a foot injury, but should be back soon. South African tighthead Sampie Swiegers is in contention for selection after his arrival in London.

Chandler Cunningham-South and Guido Petti may be due a run from the start.

But, with Alex Dombrandt [expected to miss the majority of the season with a knee ligament injury sustained in June,](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/cgevrzvnzvqo) Quins will need them all to hit the ground running.

Snarl up front, rather than style out back, is where they are lacking.

*   
[Gloucester thrash sorry Quins to go top of the Prem](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/cw305gm8j591o)

    

    *   Published 1 day ago 

## Unbeaten Bristol draw a crowd

![Image 2: Louis Rees Zammit](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/d634/live/15294f20-c0ad-11f1-b72b-c3e328aa18ed.jpg)Image source, Getty Images

Image caption, 

Rees-Zammit tops the early-season try-scoring standings, having crossed four times

Bristol chief executive Tom Tainton caught some flak earlier this year for saying the [Bears needs to think like a marketing agency, rather than a traditional rugby club,, external](https://www.bristolpost.co.uk/sport/rugby/rugby-news/bristol-bears-chief-executive-clarifies-10948316) to grow its fanbase.

The image of Louis Rees-Zammit mimicking Northampton star Henry Pollock's 'pulse-check' celebration, and the delight it sparked among fans, were evidence in his favour however.

A 20,756-strong crowd at Ashton Gate – up 5,000 on their win in the same fixture last year, partly helped by football's international break – relished a spiky performance all round from Rees-Zammit.

The Wales international could easily [have had a hat-trick in a 34-26 win over Saints,](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/cqm27ln49devo) but was body-checked by Tommy Freeman in pursuit of a final-play chip ahead, earning a penalty try and sending his opposite number on his way with a few blunt observations.

Rees-Zammit, restored to the wing after dabbling at full-back on his return from American football, has four tries already this season and Bristol, who were well in last year's play-off hunt before a dip in form after the Six Nations, are looking ominous.

The next four rounds of action – Saracens (a), Exeter (h), Leicester (h) and Bath (a) – are a big chance to dent some other top-four hopefuls.

Rees-Zammit was not the only wing on a wind-up this weekend either, by the way. Adam Radwan's gleeful celebration of his try for Leicester against former club Newcastle, marking his territory by pointing to the pitch below his studs, drew jeers from the Kingston Park crowd.

*   
[Rees-Zammit stars as Bristol power past Northampton](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/cqm27ln49devo)

    

    *   Published 1 day ago 

## Obano and Stuart stake claim for England's 'bomb squad'

![Image 3: Bath huddle up before playing Exeter](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/5137/live/4552de50-c0ad-11f1-b72b-c3e328aa18ed.jpg)Image source, Getty Images

Image caption, 

Bath took some measure of revenge after losing a Prem semi-final at home to Exeter this summer

England boss Steve Borthwick was at The Rec on Friday night.

He will have taken particular interest in one 28th-minute scrum.

Beno Obano and Will Stuart, either side of hooker Tom Dunn, made the Exeter front row look as though they were wearing skis rather than studs, sending the visitors skidding backwards at a rate of knots.

Considering Baxter's lack of game time and Bevan Rodd being ruled out of the autumn after wrist surgery, Obano may well be the back-up loosehead option to Ellis Genge for England's Nations Championship campaign.

Stuart's welcome return from an Achilles injury is likely to have him installed as the tighthead replacement behind the excellent Joe Heyes.

Borthwick may well lean into their Bath connection as he rebuilds a 'bomb squad' bench which was crucial to England's good form in 2025.

Gloucester fly-half Charlie Atkinson may well be twisting Borthwick's arm as well.

The 25-year-old has been central to the Cherry and Whites' electric start to the season.

He set up the opening try of their thrashing of Harlequins with a cute jink past Will Porter and then a pinpoint crossfield bomb for Ben Loader a couple of passages later. A hint of a dummy and a dart took Atkinson himself over for his team's fourth.

His substandard goal-kicking may count against him. Of players with a minimum of 10 kicks at goal, only Bath's Santi Carreras had a lower success-rate off the tee in 2025-26. Team-mate George Barton had kicking duties on Saturday.

But if Borthwick wants a back-up stand-off that more closely replicates the playing style of first-choice Fin Smith, Atkinson may be due promotion after three appearances for England A last season.

*   
[Bath gain revenge on Exeter to win 11-try thriller](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/c8r4vg227kvzo)

    

    *   Published 2 days ago 

## Kane more than able for Exeter

![Image 4: Kane James](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/5d14/live/813f71d0-c0ad-11f1-b72b-c3e328aa18ed.jpg)Image source, Getty Images

Image caption, 

James represented England as an under-20, but switched allegiances to play for Wales at Test level

Last year's runners-up Exeter have begun the season with successive defeats, but there was significant improvement on their opening-day defeat by Gloucester as they threatened [to climb off the canvas and overturn Bath,](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/c8r4vg227kvzo) just as they did in June's semi-final at The Rec.

A fit, firing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso - 133m carried, nine defenders beaten and two tries - was an obvious plus for the Chiefs.

But Kane James made a major step forward.

The 21-year-old Welsh international, who only made his first Prem start at the beginning of this season, was fearless at the Rec, flying into contact with relish.

As well as that wince-inducing ball-carrying, he was cleaning up on the floor, winning three turnovers.

Australia international Tom Hooper is now back in the south west, but has had a high workload switching between Chiefs and Wallabies' duties.

James has made a decent claim to holding on to his back-row spot a little longer.

## Red Bulls gathering momentum

![Image 5: Adam Radwan](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/d191/live/bf40db90-c0ad-11f1-b026-53d1506ee826.jpg)Image source, Shutterstock

Image caption, 

Adam Radwan marked his return to Newcastle with an unpopular but enthusiastic celebration

With the clock in the red and five points down on the scoreboard, Newcastle Red Bulls smuggled the ball out wide to a full-flight Christian Wade.

The 35-year-old had a corridor of space to accelerate into and 45m to cover to the tryline.

Leicester replacement Tom Whiteley just about managed to shut the gap and, a few phases later, Newcastle infringed to give away a penalty and snuff out any hope of victory.

[Like Wade's try record however,](https://www.bbc.com/sport/rugby-union/articles/c6m2r21pp7vno) it is coming for Newcastle.

After a decent showing in defeat away to champions Northampton in the opening round, Newcastle had the upper hand on Leicester for large stretches.

The visitors made more than double the number of tackles of their opponents.

The accuracy to turn possession into points is one of a number of things that will surely improve steeply as the Newcastle squad, revamped with more than 20 summer signings, gel together.

The **Rugby Football League** (**RFL**) is the governing body for [rugby league in England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_in_England "Rugby league in England").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_League#cite_note-4) Founded in 1895 as the **Northern Rugby Football Union** following 22 clubs resigning from the [Rugby Football Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union"), it changed its name in 1922 to the Rugby Football League.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_League#cite_note-5)

Based at [Sportcity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportcity "Sportcity") in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), it is responsible for organising professional competitions and, in association with the [British Amateur Rugby League Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Amateur_Rugby_League_Association "British Amateur Rugby League Association") (BARLA), the community game. It also provides [match officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RFL_match_officials "RFL match officials") for every level as well as administering the [England national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_rugby_league_team "England national rugby league team").

The Rugby Football League has been a member of the [International Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Rugby_League "International Rugby League") (IRL) since 1948 and [European Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Rugby_League "European Rugby League") (ERL) since its foundation in 2003.

## History

### Formation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_Football_League&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Formation")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Celebrating_the_birth_of_Rugby_League.jpg/250px-Celebrating_the_birth_of_Rugby_League.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Celebrating_the_birth_of_Rugby_League.jpg)

Plaque celebrating the birth of Rugby League

See also: [History of rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_rugby_league "History of rugby league")

On Tuesday 27 August 1895, as a result of an emergency meeting in [Manchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester "Manchester"), prominent Lancashire rugby clubs Broughton Rangers, Leigh, Oldham, Rochdale Hornets, St Helens, Tyldesley, Warrington, Widnes and Wigan declared that they would support their Yorkshire colleagues in their proposal to form a Northern Union.

Two days later, on Thursday 29 August 1895, representatives of 21 clubs met in the [George Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Hotel,_Huddersfield "George Hotel, Huddersfield"), Huddersfield to form the "Northern Rugby Football Union" (usually termed Northern Union or NU). Twenty clubs agreed to resign from the [Rugby Football Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_Union "Rugby Football Union"), but Dewsbury felt unable to comply with the decision. The [Cheshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire") club, Stockport, had telegraphed the meeting requesting admission to the new organisation and was duly accepted with a second Cheshire club, Runcorn, admitted at the next meeting.

The 22 clubs were:

2.   [Bradford FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford_(Park_Avenue) "Bradford (Park Avenue)") (switched to association football in 1907 and became [Bradford Park Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bradford_(Park_Avenue) "Bradford (Park Avenue)"))[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_Football_League#cite_note-6)
3.   [Brighouse Rangers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighouse_Rangers "Brighouse Rangers") (Folded in 1906, now survives as an amateur club)
4.   [Broughton Rangers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broughton_Rangers "Broughton Rangers") (Folded in 1955)
5.   [Halifax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Halifax_Panthers "Halifax Panthers")
6.   [Huddersfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huddersfield_Giants "Huddersfield Giants")
7.   [Hull FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hull_FC "Hull FC")
8.   [Hunslet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunslet_F.C._(1883) "Hunslet F.C. (1883)") (Folded in 1973 but were resurrected as a [Phoenix club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunslet_RLFC "Hunslet RLFC"))
9.   [Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leeds_Rhinos "Leeds Rhinos")
10.   [Leigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leigh_Leopards "Leigh Leopards")
11.   [Liversedge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liversedge_RFC "Liversedge RFC") (Folded in 1902, survive as an amateur club)

The **New South Wales Rugby League Ltd** (**NSWRL**) is an Australian [rugby league football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_football "Rugby league football") competition operator in [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_in_New_South_Wales "Rugby league in New South Wales") and the [Australian Capital Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Capital_Territory "Australian Capital Territory") and is a member of the [Australian Rugby League Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Rugby_League_Commission "Australian Rugby League Commission").

It was registered on 21 December 1983[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_Rugby_League#cite_note-1) and succeeded the New South Wales Rugby Football League which had been formed in Sydney on 8 August 1907.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_Rugby_League#cite_note-ARL2007annrep-2) The NSWRFL and then NSWRL operated the premier rugby league club competitions for Sydney, then New South Wales and then Australia from [1908](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSWRFL_season_1908 "NSWRFL season 1908") to [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSWRL_season_1994 "NSWRL season 1994"). The organisation administers the [New South Wales rugby league team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_rugby_league_team "New South Wales rugby league team") for [State of Origin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Origin "State of Origin").

## New South Wales Rugby League clubs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=New_South_Wales_Rugby_League&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Current New South Wales members")]

Of all of the club in New South Wales, some are some who field teams in the [NRL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League "National Rugby League"), [New South Wales Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSW_Cup "NSW Cup") and [New South Wales Jersey Flegg Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_Flegg_Cup "Jersey Flegg Cup"), and there are some who no longer field teams in the NRL, but continue to field teams in the [New South Wales Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSW_Cup "NSW Cup") and [New South Wales Jersey Flegg Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jersey_Flegg_Cup "Jersey Flegg Cup").

The **Rugby League World Cup 9s** was an international tournament played in the [rugby league nines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines "Rugby league nines") tournament.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Cup_9s#cite_note-1)

The inaugural World Cup 9s took place on 18 and 19 October 2019 at the [Bankwest Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankwest_Stadium "Bankwest Stadium") in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales "New South Wales"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"). The women's competition was won by [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_women's_national_rugby_league_team "New Zealand women's national rugby league team"), and the men's competition by the hosts [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_national_rugby_league_team "Australia national rugby league team").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Cup_9s#cite_note-2) The tournament, like the [XIII's tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Cup "Rugby League World Cup"), was intended to be held every four years. However the 2023 tournament, which was due to be held in Australia, was cancelled due to the [New South Wales Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_New_South_Wales "Government of New South Wales") withdrawing support after the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Australia "COVID-19 pandemic in Australia").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Cup_9s#cite_note-3)

The **Rugby League World Cup 9s** was an international tournament played in the [rugby league nines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines "Rugby league nines") tournament.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Cup_9s#cite_note-1)

The inaugural World Cup 9s took place on 18 and 19 October 2019 at the [Bankwest Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bankwest_Stadium "Bankwest Stadium") in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales "New South Wales"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"). The women's competition was won by [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_women's_national_rugby_league_team "New Zealand women's national rugby league team"), and the men's competition by the hosts [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_national_rugby_league_team "Australia national rugby league team").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Cup_9s#cite_note-2) The tournament, like the [XIII's tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Cup "Rugby League World Cup"), was intended to be held every four years. However the 2023 tournament, which was due to be held in Australia, was cancelled due to the [New South Wales Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_New_South_Wales "Government of New South Wales") withdrawing support after the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Australia "COVID-19 pandemic in Australia").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Cup_9s#cite_note-3)

**Rugby league sevens** (or simply **sevens**) is a seven-a-side derivative of [rugby league football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"), which is usually a thirteen-a-side sport. The game is substantially the same as full [rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league"), with some rule changes and shorter games. Sevens is usually played in festivals, as its shorter game play allows for a tournament to be completed in a day or over a single weekend.

As well as being played by club sides, rugby league sevens is particularly popular with social teams, formed in the workplace or from the patrons of a public house for example, as it is often difficult in these places to form a full squad of 13 players and four substitutes of regular players. Some tournaments prefer to play [rugby league nines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines "Rugby league nines") (rugby league with nine players on each side) to distinguish it from [rugby union sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union_sevens "Rugby union sevens").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The game of [rugby sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_sevens "Rugby sevens") dates back to its invention by [Ned Haig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ned_Haig "Ned Haig") in [Melrose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melrose,_Scotland "Melrose, Scotland") in the [Scottish Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Borders "Scottish Borders") in 1883, just over a decade before the schism in [rugby football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_football "Rugby football") in 1895, which led to the creation of rugby league and [rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union"). However, rugby sevens did not spread outside Scotland before the 1920s. That said, the larger part of Scotland's rugby league players have come from Borders backgrounds.

The record rugby league sevens attendance remains the 80,000 that attended a 1933 match between Australia and England at Roundhay Park in Leeds. This match was also attended by English royalty.

The first rugby _league_ sevens tournament was played in Australia in 1961.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-centofrl1-1)

The major tournament was the [World Sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens "Rugby League World Sevens") played prior to the beginning of the [National Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League "National Rugby League") season in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), Australia. That tournament has been suspended but sevens is played around the world at different levels from junior teams to international ones. Sevens is considered to be a good tool to increase the skills of players and to help emerging rugby league nations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-nrlnewsking1-2)

## Playing area

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Playing area")]

Sevens is played on a standard [rugby league playing field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_playing_field "Rugby league playing field") as defined in Section 1 of the _International Laws of the Game_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-ILG-3)

## Teams

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Teams")]

Teams are composed of three forwards, one half and three backs.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4)

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Rules")]

Sevens follows the [rules of 13-a-side rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_of_rugby_league "Laws of rugby league") with exceptions. Each rugby league nation is at liberty to adopt a modified version of international rugby league rules for their own domestic competitions; as a result the rules of rugby league sevens can vary too, even before changes implemented by competition organisers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-rl1908rulesvary-5)

Matches have two halves of seven minutes.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4) Unlimited substitutions are allowed from a squad totalling 12 players.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4) In sevens, smaller [scrums](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scrum_(rugby) "Scrum (rugby)"), formed from the three forwards on each team, are formed.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4) All kicks for goal should be [drop kicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drop_kick "Drop kick") in sevens.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4) After points have been scored a tap kick restart is taken by the non-scoring side.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unisport7rules-4)

The [World Sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_League_World_Sevens "Rugby League World Sevens"), the world's premier sevens event while it operated, had two 7 minute halves up to and including the semi-finals with extra time played in the event of tie at the end normal time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-2020upnunder7s-6) The final was longer with two 10-minute halves. In 2004, the World Sevens tackle limit was reduced from 6 to 4.

## Major sevens festivals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_sevens&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Major sevens festivals")]

*   World Sevens was suspended in 2005 because NRL teams were reluctant to field their star players, resulting in dwindling spectator numbers.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-nrlnewsking1-2)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unlimgsteven1-7) Play resumed
*   Actor [Russell Crowe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russell_Crowe "Russell Crowe") hosts the [Orara Valley Axemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orara_Valley_Axemen "Orara Valley Axemen") Sevens Tournament at Coffs Harbour on the New South Wales North Coast.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_sevens#cite_note-unlimgsteven1-7) This tournament is participated in by teams representing countries of the world, local clubs and a few clubs from Brisbane, Australia. In 2005 the [Souths Logan Magpies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Souths_Logan_Magpies "Souths Logan Magpies") from the [Queensland Wizard Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland_Cup "Queensland Cup") and the [Gold Coast Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_Titans "Gold Coast Titans"), who entered the [NRL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League "National Rugby League") in 2007, were two well known clubs that participated.
*   [Latino Rugby League Sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latino_Rugby_League_Sevens "Latino Rugby League Sevens")

**Rugby league nines** (or simply **nines**) is a version of [rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league") football played with nine players on each side. The game is substantially the same as full rugby league, with some differences in [rules](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_of_rugby_league "Laws of rugby league") and shorter games. Nines is usually played in festivals, as its shorter game play allows for a tournament to be completed in a day or over a single weekend.

In July 2021, [International Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Rugby_League "International Rugby League") (IRL) chair [Troy Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Troy_Grant "Troy Grant") stated that the organisation was considering a bid for rugby league nines to be played at the [2032 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2032_Summer_Olympics "2032 Summer Olympics") in Brisbane. [Rugby sevens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_sevens "Rugby sevens"), a similarly-condensed version of [rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union"), has been a core Olympic event since [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines#cite_note-1)

## Laws

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rugby_league_nines&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Laws")]

The laws of the game are the same as [standard rugby league laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laws_of_rugby_league "Laws of rugby league") with the following exceptions.

*   Each team is allowed a squad of up to fifteen players, with no more than nine players on the field at any time. Unlimited substitutions are allowed from a named bench of four players.
*   The match lasts for 18 minutes, divided into two halves of 9 minutes. There is no half time interval but teams are allowed a maximum of 1 minute to change ends. Each half starts with a place kick.
*   Scrums consist of no more than 5 forwards, with a maximum 3 in the front row and 2 in the second row. When the ball is in the scrum no more than 4 players from each team shall act as backs. The ball must emerge from behind the feet of the second row.
*   Conversions after a successful try take the form of drop kicks. Players from the team that has conceded the score do not have to retire behind the try line but must not interfere with any conversion attempt.
*   When points have been scored the team against which points have been scored will restart the game with a tap restart from the centre of the half-way line.
*   When a team is awarded a penalty then play must proceed by way of a tap 10-metres in advance of where the infringement took place.
*   In the event of misconduct by a player the referee can suspend for 5 minutes. In the [Carnegie Floodlit Nines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carnegie_Floodlit_Nines "Carnegie Floodlit Nines"), a major nines competition, this has been reduced to 2 minutes.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines#cite_note-SL14906-04-08-09-2)

The **NRL Nines** is a [rugby league nines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_nines "Rugby league nines") competition, normally held during the [NRL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL "NRL") preseason each year. It was initially held in [Auckland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auckland "Auckland"), [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), between 2014 and 2017 before going on hiatus.

Returning in 2020, hosting duties moved to [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth"), [Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Australia "Western Australia"), before being cancelled in 2021. The series has not returned since.

## Competition format

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Competition format")]

### Auckland (2014–2017)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Auckland (2014–2017)")]

Two national women's teams compete in one section of the tournament and sixteen NRL club men's teams compete in the other. Each of the men's squad must include at least 12 of their top 25 players in their squad, and at least one marquee player. The winner of the men's tournament received [AUD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUD "AUD")$500,000 with a total prize pool of AUD$2,250,000. In the first four editions, the competition has had eight different finalists and four different winners, though the 2016 title was later stripped from the Parramatta Eels for breaching the salary cap.

Since 2015 the [Kiwiferns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_women's_national_rugby_league_team "New Zealand women's national rugby league team") and the [Jillaroos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_women's_national_rugby_league_team "Australia women's national rugby league team") also competed in a three-game series, with the Kiwiferns winning the series 2-1. These games are played during the final stages of the men's tournament and allow the male players more of a break between their games while providing a broader tournament. Also in 2015, the pools were given traditional Maori names that were chosen by a public vote and were: [Rangitoto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rangitoto "Rangitoto"), [Waiheke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waiheke "Waiheke"), [Piha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piha "Piha") and [Hunua Ranges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunua_Ranges "Hunua Ranges").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-2)

### Perth (2020)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Perth (2020)")]

The women's teams were [NRL Women's Premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Women's_Premiership "NRL Women's Premiership") sides instead of national teams.

### Series Cancellations (2021–2024)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Series Cancellations (2021–2024)")]

The 2021 series was cancelled entirely, not due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Australia "COVID-19 pandemic in Australia"), but due to an overly-crowded preseason schedule.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-4)

When the 2022 Fixtures list was released by the NRL, it included no mention of the [World Club Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Club_Challenge "World Club Challenge") or NRL Nines competitions.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-5)

The [World Club Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Club_Challenge "World Club Challenge") did make its return in 2023, and again in 2024, but the NRL Nines competition was absent for both years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-6)

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=NRL_Nines&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Rules")]

There are a number of rule variations that are implemented to ensure the games are faster and to ensure fewer delays and stoppages.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Nines#cite_note-7)

The major rule changes that differ from regular NRL games are:

*   Two nine-minute halves with a two-minute half time period.
*   Nine players a side with five unlimited interchange players (six interchanges in 2014).
*   Scrums are only formed after a double knock on, with attacking teams electing which side to feed the ball.
*   No video referee, with one on-field referee, two touch judges and two in-goal judges.
*   Five minute golden try period in qualifying rounds with the match deemed a draw if there is no score, while unlimited golden try for the finals.
*   A tap restart takes place after a 40/20.
*   Five points for a try scored in the bonus zone under the posts, with two point drop kick conversion attempts.
*   The scoring team will have a drop-kick kick-off at the half way mark to restart play.
*   Three minute sin bins (Five in 2014).
*   Five tackles in a set.

The **National Rugby League** (also known as the **NRL Telstra Premiership** for sponsorship reasons) is a professional [rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league") competition in [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania "Oceania") which is currently contested by 16 teams based in Australia (in [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales "New South Wales"), [Queensland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queensland "Queensland"), [Victoria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_(state) "Victoria (state)"), and the [Australian Capital Territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Capital_Territory "Australian Capital Territory")), and 1 team based in [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"). Expansion teams based in [Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Australia "Western Australia") ([Perth Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth_Bears "Perth Bears")) and [Papua New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_New_Guinea "Papua New Guinea") ([Papua New Guinea Chiefs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_New_Guinea_Chiefs "Papua New Guinea Chiefs")) are set to enter the competition in 2027 and 2028 respectively.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-2)

Tracing its origins back to the [New South Wales Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_Rugby_League "New South Wales Rugby League"), which formed in 1908, premier rugby league competition in Australia had gone through numerous iterations, most notably during the [Super League war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_war "Super League war") in the 1990s,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-3) which resulted in the NRL being formed in 1998 as a joint partnership between the [Australian Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Rugby_League_Commission "Australian Rugby League Commission") (ARL) and the [News Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_Corporation "News Corporation")-controlled [Super League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_(Australia) "Super League (Australia)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-4) The partnership was dissolved in 2012, with control of the NRL going to the re-constituted ARL, which was re-structured with an independent board of directors and renamed the [Australian Rugby League Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Rugby_League_Commission "Australian Rugby League Commission").

Each NRL season typically runs from March to October, with each team playing 24 matches. The first-placed team at the end of the regular season are awarded the [J. J. Giltinan Shield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._J._Giltinan_Shield "J. J. Giltinan Shield") for winning the [minor premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minor_premiership "Minor premiership"). This is followed by a [finals series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_finals_system "NRL finals system") contested between the top eight placed teams from the regular season, which determines the two teams to compete in the [NRL Grand Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Grand_Final "NRL Grand Final") held at [Stadium Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium_Australia "Stadium Australia"). The team that wins the match are awarded the [Provan-Summons Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#Provan-Summons_trophy) in recognition for becoming the [premiers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#Title_winners) of the season,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-5) and qualifies them to compete in the [World Club Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Club_Challenge "World Club Challenge") against the champions of the English [Super League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League "Super League").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-6) The reigning premiers are the [Sydney Roosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Roosters "Sydney Roosters"), having won their sixteenth premiership in the [2026 NRL season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_NRL_season "2026 NRL season").

The NRL is the richest rugby league football league and overall rugby league (including [rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union") and [rugby league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league "Rugby league")) in the world by revenue. It is also the [31st richest sports league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_professional_sports_leagues_by_revenue "List of professional sports leagues by revenue") in the world and the second richest in Australia behind the [Australian Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Football_League "Australian Football League").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Rugby_League&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of the National Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_National_Rugby_League "History of the National Rugby League")

See also: [Rugby league in Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_league_in_Australia "Rugby league in Australia") and [List of NRL records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_NRL_records "List of NRL records")

### Origin and establishment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Rugby_League&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origin and establishment")]

The [New South Wales Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_Rugby_League "New South Wales Rugby League") ran the major rugby league competition of New South Wales from its [inception in 1908](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_NSWRFL_season "1908 NSWRFL season") until [1994](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_Rugby_League_season_1994 "New South Wales Rugby League season 1994"). Following the introduction of a new format for interstate rugby league, the [State of Origin series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Origin_series "State of Origin series") in 1980, the decade of the 1980s brought about expansion of the [NSWRL premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_Rugby_League_premiership "New South Wales Rugby League premiership"), with the introduction of commercial sponsorship, the [Winfield Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winfield_Cup "Winfield Cup"), and the addition of non-Sydney-based teams, [Canberra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra_Raiders "Canberra Raiders") and [Illawarra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illawarra_Steelers "Illawarra Steelers") in 1982.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-8) Although this move brought more interest in the competition statewide in [New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales "New South Wales"), it would spell the beginning of the demise of some of the traditional Sydney-based clubs, as well as having a negative effect on the [Brisbane Rugby League premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane_Rugby_League_premiership "Brisbane Rugby League premiership"). Following the 1983 season, Sydney foundation club [Newtown Jets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newtown_Jets "Newtown Jets") were ultimately forced to withdraw from the competition because of financial difficulties.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-9)

Further expansion of the league followed in [1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_South_Wales_Rugby_League_season_1988 "New South Wales Rugby League season 1988"), with another three teams based outside Sydney introduced to the competition; the [Newcastle Knights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newcastle_Knights "Newcastle Knights") and the first two Queensland teams, the [Brisbane Broncos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane_Broncos "Brisbane Broncos") and [Gold Coast-Tweed Giants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast-Tweed_Giants "Gold Coast-Tweed Giants").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-10) The Brisbane and Newcastle sides proved to be successful and popular and paved the way towards a push for a truly national competition.

This was attempted in [1995](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_ARL_season "1995 ARL season") with control of the premiership passing from the NSWRFL to the [Australian Rugby League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Rugby_League "Australian Rugby League") (ARL), who invited four more teams from outside NSW to participate in 1995. Ultimately, this competition failed, but in its demise, the National Rugby League was born, incorporating the traditional Sydney clubs, successfully compelling the Sydney market to follow the newly created national competition.

See also: [Super League war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_war "Super League war")

The prospect of a truly national rugby league competition in addition to the introduction of pay television in Australia attracted the attention of global media organisation, [News Corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_Corporation "News Corporation"), and it followed that professional rugby league was shaken to its very foundations in the mid-1990s with the advent of the [Super League war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_war "Super League war"). Initially a conflict over broadcasting rights, it became a dispute as to who controlled the sport and which traditional clubs would survive into the new national era, as News Limited formed their own [Super League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_League_(Australia) "Super League (Australia)") and admitted some former ARL clubs, poaching players from the original ARL league with high salaries. With twenty-two teams of highly varying quality playing in two competitions that year, crowd attendances and corporate sponsorships were spread very thinly,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-rleague1-11) and many teams found themselves in financial difficulty. The ARL undertook moves to invite the traditional clubs that had moved to the Super League competition back into a re-unified competition. Following a period of negotiation with News Corporation, on 23 September 1997, the ARL announced that it was forming a new company to conduct the competition in 1998. On 7 October, News' Manaaki Ranginui announced that he was confident that there would be a single competition in 1998. On 19 December, representatives of clubs affiliated with the Australian Rugby League gathered at the [Sydney Football Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Football_Stadium_(1988) "Sydney Football Stadium (1988)") to decide whether to accept News Limited's offer of a settlement – eventually voting in favour by 36 votes to 4.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-12) As a result, in the following months the National Rugby League, jointly owned by the [ARL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Rugby_League "Australian Rugby League") and News Limited, was formed.

It was announced that the inaugural National Rugby League (NRL) season of [1998](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_NRL_season "1998 NRL season") would have 20 teams competing, 19 remaining Super League and ARL teams plus the [Melbourne Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Storm "Melbourne Storm"), who were created by Super League for their 1998 season. Clubs on both sides of the war were shut down. Super League decided to close the [Hunter Mariners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunter_Mariners "Hunter Mariners") and the financially ruined [Perth Reds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth_Reds "Perth Reds"), who were $10 million in debt at the end of 1997,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] while the ARL decided to close down the [South Queensland Crushers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Queensland_Crushers "South Queensland Crushers"), who were also in severe financial trouble.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Additionally, at the end of 1998 the NRL decided to close down former Super League club, the [Adelaide Rams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelaide_Rams "Adelaide Rams") and former ARL club, the [Gold Coast Chargers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_Chargers "Gold Coast Chargers"), despite the Gold Coast franchise being one of the few clubs to make a profit during the Super League war.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

### 1998–2002: Rationalisation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Rugby_League&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1998–2002: Rationalisation")]

One condition of the peace agreement between the ARL and News Limited was that there would be a 14-team competition in 2000. The 20 clubs that played in 1998 would be assessed on various items such as sponsorship, crowds, on-field success and the like. It was also announced that clubs that merged would receive a large sum of money, as well as a guaranteed position in the 2000 NRL Competition. The [St. George Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George_Dragons "St. George Dragons") and the [Illawarra Steelers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illawarra_Steelers "Illawarra Steelers") were the first clubs to take up the offer, forming the joint-venture [St. George Illawarra Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George_Illawarra_Dragons "St. George Illawarra Dragons") at the end of the 1998 season.

The [1999 Grand Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_NRL_season "1999 NRL season") brought about a new official world record attendance for a game of rugby league. 107,999 spectators saw the [Melbourne Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Storm "Melbourne Storm") defeat the newly created [St. George Illawarra Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George_Illawarra_Dragons "St. George Illawarra Dragons") in the decider at [Stadium Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stadium_Australia "Stadium Australia").

[Balmain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balmain_Tigers "Balmain Tigers") and [Western Suburbs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Suburbs_Magpies "Western Suburbs Magpies") formed the joint-venture club, the [Wests Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wests_Tigers "Wests Tigers") at the end of 1999, while [North Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sydney_Bears "North Sydney Bears") and [Manly Warringah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manly_Warringah_Sea_Eagles "Manly Warringah Sea Eagles") created the ill-fated [Northern Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Eagles "Northern Eagles"). As part of another image makeover, a number of teams also released new club logos. The most notable of these was the Sydney Roosters, dropping the _City_ section of their name for the 2000 season and beyond. [Souths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sydney_Rabbitohs "South Sydney Rabbitohs") were controversially axed from the competition at the end of 1999 for failing to meet the criteria.

This move was highly controversial, and on 12 November 2000, about 80,000 marched in protest at their continued exclusion. South Sydney challenged the decision in the Federal Court, claiming that the NRL agreement was exclusionary, intended to unfairly exclude South Sydney, and breached the Trade Practices Act. Justice Paul Finn ruled that the agreement did not specifically exclude any club and dismissed the Rabbitohs' claims for reinstatement into the national competition. Souths appealed this decision and were re-admitted into the competition in 2002.

The Auckland Warriors experienced much financial hardship in the early part of the decade, ultimately collapsing before being resurrected as the New Zealand Warriors for the 2001 season. They made the grand final in 2002 and then again in 2011, losing both encounters to the Sydney Roosters and the re-instated Manly Warringah Sea Eagles, respectively.

In 2001, Australia's largest telecommunications provider, Telstra, became the naming rights sponsor of the NRL, with the competition's name becoming the NRL Telstra Premiership. [David Gallop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Gallop "David Gallop") took over the CEO role from [David Moffett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Moffett "David Moffett") in 2002.

In 2001, the NRL Grand Final started to be played on Sunday nights, a shift from the traditional Sunday afternoon slot used for over a decade prior.

### 2003–2010: Record popularity, expansion and centenary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Rugby_League&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2003–2010: Record popularity, expansion and centenary")]

The 2003 season was widely regarded as the most successful since the beginning of the National Rugby League in 1998. The Manly Warringah Rugby League Football Club took over the NRL licence from the [Northern Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Eagles "Northern Eagles") franchise, after the financial bankruptcy of the North Sydney faction made the joint-venture untenable. The [Penrith Panthers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penrith_Panthers "Penrith Panthers") rose from the bottom of the table to win the Premiership, while the Brisbane club returned to [Lang Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suncorp_Stadium "Suncorp Stadium") mid-year. Season 2004 proved even more successful than 2003, with the [North Queensland Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Queensland_Cowboys "North Queensland Cowboys") going from 11th position in 2003 to third in 2004, narrowly missing out on a maiden Grand Final berth.

Crowd average records were broken in 2003, 2004 and 2005.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-rleague1-11) In 2005, the NRL reached record levels of popularity for its competition. Total crowds for the competition season almost reached the figures for the last year of the competition conducted by the ARL competition of 1995, prior to the Super League war. The average attendance record remained until 2010.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-rleague1-11) From 2004 to 2005, there was a 39% increase in sponsorship, a 41% increase in merchandise royalties, and a 12% increase in playing participation.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-13) In 2005, [Business Review Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRW_(magazine) "BRW (magazine)") ranked the NRL 497 in revenue of Australian private companies, with revenue of A$66.1m (+7%) with 35 employees. In 2004, Canterbury-Bankstown put a year of turmoil and disgrace in the aftermath of the alleged rape scandal to hold the NRL trophy aloft and give the club its first premiership since 1995. In 2005, a record national audience of 4.1 million tuned in to watch the grand final between the [Wests Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wests_Tigers "Wests Tigers") and the [North Queensland Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Queensland_Cowboys "North Queensland Cowboys").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-14)

The [2006 Grand Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_NRL_Grand_Final "2006 NRL Grand Final") was won by the [Brisbane Broncos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane_Broncos "Brisbane Broncos") over the [Melbourne Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Storm "Melbourne Storm"), 15–8. The matchup was a significant milestone in the history of the NRL, as two interstate teams (teams not from New South Wales, the "heartland" of the NRL) contested the grand final for the first time. In the city of Melbourne, whose team was playing in their second grand final, the game's television ratings were higher than in Sydney, where the game was played.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-15)

In its tenth season, the NRL returned to having a club based on the [Gold Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast,_Queensland "Gold Coast, Queensland"), Queensland, with the inclusion of the [Gold Coast Titans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_Titans "Gold Coast Titans"). The Titans were the first professional sporting team to occupy the Gold Coast since 1998, when the [Gold Coast Chargers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_Chargers "Gold Coast Chargers") were one of the teams removed during the NRL's rationalisation process between the end of the Super League war and the 2000 season.

The 2007 season saw the return of Monday Night Football and the inclusion of two Friday night games. Both of which turned out to be ratings successes. Another change from the previous seasons was a reduction in the number of byes per team in the season. With an odd number of teams contesting between 2002 and 2006, the draw meant that at least one team would have to have a bye each weekend. With the inclusion of the 16th team for the 2007 season, the National Rugby League had the option of reverting to the system used between 2000 and 2001, where every team played each round. That system was not used, however, as teams were given a single bye during the year—grouped in periods—that assisted clubs manage representative fixtures.

The opening round saw two matches at Brisbane's [Lang Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suncorp_Stadium "Suncorp Stadium"), the first featuring reigning champions Brisbane against fellow Queensland side North Queensland, while the second match featured the new club, the Gold Coast, playing St. George Illawarra. The weather during the middle of the season was less than ideal, with cyclonic conditions severely affecting many NRL games played in Sydney and Newcastle.

The 2007 finals series saw the [South Sydney Rabbitohs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sydney_Rabbitohs "South Sydney Rabbitohs") return to finals football for the first time in decades. The season culminated on 30 September 2007, with the grand final contested between Manly and Melbourne. Melbourne won the title 34–8, and the grand final achieved the honour of being the most-watched television show in Australia in 2007.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-autogenerated1-16)

Throughout 2008, the NRL celebrated 100 years since rugby league was introduced into Australia, with several initiatives to recognise the important milestone, including an extensive marketing campaign called the 'Centenary of Rugby League'. The competition began in March, with a special Heritage round held in mid-April, coinciding with the first round of competition played in 1908.

At a Gala event on 17 April 2008, the [Team of the Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Rugby_League's_Team_of_the_Century "Australian Rugby League's Team of the Century") was announced, being:

*   Full-back: [Clive Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Churchill "Clive Churchill")
*   Wingers: [Ken Irvine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Irvine "Ken Irvine"), [Brian Bevan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Bevan "Brian Bevan")
*   Centres: [Reg Gasnier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reg_Gasnier "Reg Gasnier"), [Mal Meninga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mal_Meninga "Mal Meninga")
*   Five-eighth: [Wally Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wally_Lewis "Wally Lewis")
*   Half-back: [Andrew Johns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Johns "Andrew Johns")
*   Lock: [John Raper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnny_Raper "Johnny Raper")*   Second Row: [Norm Provan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norm_Provan "Norm Provan"), [Ron Coote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Coote "Ron Coote")
*   Props: [Arthur Beetson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Beetson "Arthur Beetson"), [Duncan Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Hall "Duncan Hall")
*   Hooker: [Noel Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noel_Kelly_(rugby_league) "Noel Kelly (rugby league)")
*   Reserves: [Graeme Langlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graeme_Langlands "Graeme Langlands"), [Dally Messenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dally_Messenger "Dally Messenger"), [Bob Fulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Fulton "Bob Fulton"), [Frank Burge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Burge "Frank Burge")
*   Coach: [Jack Gibson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Gibson_(rugby_league) "Jack Gibson (rugby league)").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-17)

For the second year in a row, the grand final was played between the Melbourne Storm and the Manly Warringah Sea Eagles, in the NRL's first-ever twilight decider. The Manly club took out the premiership game 40–0, setting the record for the highest winning margin in a grand final (although the club formerly known as St. George Dragons were beaten 38–0 in 1975, and using the modern point scale of 4-point tries, this would amount to 46–0) Furthermore, it was the first time a team had been kept scoreless in a Grand Final since 1978.

The 2009 season marked the beginning of the second century of rugby league in Australia. The [grand final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NRL_Grand_Final "2009 NRL Grand Final") that year was played between the [Parramatta Eels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parramatta_Eels "Parramatta Eels") and once again [Melbourne Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Storm "Melbourne Storm"). Melbourne defeated Parramatta 23 – 16 to win the premiership, taking the club to two premierships out of the previous four grand finals for the Melbourne side.

In 2010, the Inaugural All Stars Match was held on 13 February, in conjunction with the Sorry Day reconciliation anniversary, to promote rugby league's long association and involvement with the Aboriginal community. The first match saw the Indigenous All Stars beat the NRL All Stars 16–12. The success of this event has seen it become a recurring fixture on the rugby league calendar with Queensland awarded the hosting rights for the next three years.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-18)

The 29th State of Origin series was also played, featuring the world's first live free-to-air 3D TV broadcast.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-19) Queensland later made further history by winning an unprecedented fifth series in a row, and winning the 2010 series by a scoreline of 3–0, their first Origin whitewash since 1995.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-20)

In 2010, the NRL set a record total season average attendance of 17,367 per game and a record total season aggregate attendance of 3,490,778.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-22)

During the 2010 finals series, the second qualifying match between the [Wests Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wests_Tigers "Wests Tigers") and [Sydney Roosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Roosters "Sydney Roosters") became the first McIntyre system final to go into extra time, with the One Hundred Minute Epic described in media circles as one of the greatest of the modern era.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-23)

The 2010 [grand final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NRL_Grand_Final "2010 NRL Grand Final") was played between the [St. George Illawarra Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._George_Illawarra_Dragons "St. George Illawarra Dragons") and the [Sydney Roosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Roosters "Sydney Roosters"). St. George Illawarra won 32–8. This was the first premiership won by the club in its eleven-year existence and the first time in 31 years for the St. George part of the joint venture.

### 2010–2019: Establishment of the ARLC

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Rugby_League&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2010–2019: Establishment of the ARLC")]

After several years of preparation and build-up, on 14 December 2010, the Australian Rugby League and News Corporation agreed upon a constitutional framework, paving the way for the establishment of a new and independent commission to govern the sport in Australia. The negotiations of such a framework became drawn out over establishing details, primarily of sponsorship, media rights, funding of state bodies, funding of the [Melbourne Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Storm "Melbourne Storm"), debate over News Ltd private ownership of clubs, and also of individual appointments to the new body. The 2011 grand final was contested between the [Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manly-Warringah_Sea_Eagles "Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles") and the [New Zealand Warriors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_Warriors "New Zealand Warriors"). This was the second grand final involving the New Zealand Warriors. Manly recorded a 24–10 win, claiming their second premiership under head coach [Des Hasler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Hasler "Des Hasler").

On 10 February 2012, the independent commission, known as the [Australian Rugby League Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Rugby_League_Commission "Australian Rugby League Commission") assumed control of all levels of the game, replacing former state based boards and assuming full control of the NRL from the NRL partnership (comprising the previous ARL board and [News Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_Corp_Australia "News Corp Australia")).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-24) The current Chairman is Peter V'landys AM. The 2012 Grand Final involved the [Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury-Bankstown_Bulldogs "Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs") and the [Melbourne Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Storm "Melbourne Storm"). This was the first time since 2008 that the first and second-placed teams contested the grand final. The [Melbourne Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Storm "Melbourne Storm") recorded a 14–4 victory, thus achieving their second premiership and claiming some vengeance for the stripped premierships.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/75/Dragons_vs_Roosters%2C_Anzac_Day_2018.jpg/250px-Dragons_vs_Roosters%2C_Anzac_Day_2018.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dragons_vs_Roosters,_Anzac_Day_2018.jpg)

Pre-match formalities taking place prior to the Dragons vs Roosters Anzac Day clash in 2018

The 2013 season saw the resurgence of foundation clubs, the [Sydney Roosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Roosters "Sydney Roosters") and the [South Sydney Rabbitohs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sydney_Rabbitohs "South Sydney Rabbitohs"), with both clubs finishing first and second place respectively. The NRL was also left with a black eye after the [Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronulla-Sutherland_Sharks "Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks") were [caught using performance-enhancing substances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronulla-Sutherland_Sharks_supplements_saga "Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks supplements saga") by [ASADA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Sports_Anti-Doping_Authority "Australian Sports Anti-Doping Authority") dating back to 2011. The 2013 Grand Final was played between the [Sydney Roosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Roosters "Sydney Roosters") and the [Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manly-Warringah_Sea_Eagles "Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles") with the Roosters recording a 26–18 victory.

The 2014 season started with the introduction of the Auckland Nines and was marred by the handing down of a million-dollar fine to the [Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronulla-Sutherland_Sharks "Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks") for their role in the ASADA scandal, while head coach Shane Flanagan was suspended for the entirety of the 2014 season. The 2014 Grand Final was contested by the [South Sydney Rabbitohs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sydney_Rabbitohs "South Sydney Rabbitohs") and the [Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canterbury-Bankstown_Bulldogs "Canterbury-Bankstown Bulldogs"). This was South Sydney's first grand final appearance since 1971. South Sydney would break their 43-year premiership drought with a 30–6 victory.

The 2015 season saw the return of the Queensland juggernauts, the [North Queensland Cowboys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Queensland_Cowboys "North Queensland Cowboys") and the [Brisbane Broncos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane_Broncos "Brisbane Broncos"), who would finish inside the top four and contest the 2015 Grand Final. The 2015 Grand Final is considered by many to be the greatest grand final of all time, as a high-intensity match ended in dramatic circumstances when North Queensland scored as the full-time siren sounded. Johnathan Thurston would miss the conversion from the sideline as the ball hit the post, thus sending the match into golden point, the first golden point grand final. Ben Hunt would drop the ball on the kick-off and hand the North Queensland side the chance to win, which was converted as Johnathan Thurston successfully kicked a field goal to win the match 17–16.

The 2016 season saw the [Melbourne Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Storm "Melbourne Storm") return to the minor premiership position while the [Canberra Raiders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canberra_Raiders "Canberra Raiders") returned to the top four for the first time since 2003. The [Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronulla-Sutherland_Sharks "Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks") and reigning premiers North Queensland would fill out the top four. The season continued a trend of the minor premiership not being decided to the final round, the fourth consecutive year. The 2016 Grand Final was contested between the Melbourne Storm and the [Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cronulla-Sutherland_Sharks "Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks"). It was Cronulla's fourth grand final appearance, and the seventh for Melbourne. The match was a tight affair and was not settled until after the siren had sounded. The Cronulla-Sutherland claimed their first premiership, ending a 49-year drought by a score of 14–12.

Following the success generated by the [2017 Women's Rugby League World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Women's_Rugby_League_World_Cup "2017 Women's Rugby League World Cup"), a [national women's league](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NRL_Women's_Premiership "NRL Women's Premiership") was established, and the [first season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_NRL_Women's_season "2018 NRL Women's season") commenced in September 2018, comprising four clubs aligned to existing NRL clubs.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-25)

### 2020–2021: COVID-affected seasons

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Rugby_League&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2020–2021: COVID-affected seasons")]

On 22 March 2020, during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), the NRL became one of the last major sports in the world to continue playing games. Following the imposition of the first COVID-19 restrictions, the NRL initially announced it would be moving forward with the season.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-26) The decision prompted a wave of condemnation online, including from Australian personalities and sportspeople.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-27) The following day after Queensland closed its borders, the NRL announced that the season would have to be suspended indefinitely.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-28) It was feared that some teams would not survive this period without income, as it was foreseen as a financial catastrophe.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-30)

On 9 April 2020, ARL Commissioner [Wayne Pearce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_Pearce "Wayne Pearce") announced the NRL would return on 28 May.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-31) The announcement came under heavy criticism from the [Government of New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_New_South_Wales "Government of New South Wales") and health officials, with Premier [Gladys Berejiklian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gladys_Berejiklian "Gladys Berejiklian") saying she had not approved a return.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-guard-green-light-32) However, the NRL released documents signed by NSW Police Commissioner Mick Fuller, showing approval for the NRL to continue without crowds.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-guard-green-light-32) The competition ended up kicking off on that date, with the [Parramatta Eels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parramatta_Eels "Parramatta Eels") defeating the [Brisbane Broncos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane_Broncos "Brisbane Broncos") 34–6 at [Lang Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lang_Park "Lang Park") behind closed doors.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-33) The match drew the highest TV ratings for a regular season game since 2014.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-34) The NRL returned a full two weeks before any other sport in Australia, and were the first sport to return to play worldwide that actually ceased play.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-35)

In October 2021, after months of speculation, the NRL and the ARLC announced that the competition would expand to 17 teams, with the admission of the [Dolphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolphins_(NRL) "Dolphins (NRL)"), based out of the suburb of Redcliffe in greater Brisbane, for the 2023 season.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-36)

### 2022 – present: Further expansion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=National_Rugby_League&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2022 – present: Further expansion")]

Following the introduction of the Dolphins in 2023, NRL executives spoke openly about the desire to further expand the competition. On 12 March 2023, reports emerged that the ARL Commission was working towards a 20-team competition, and sought to achieve this target before the [2032 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2032_Summer_Olympics "2032 Summer Olympics") in Brisbane.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-37) ARLC CEO [Andrew Abdo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Abdo "Andrew Abdo") and chairman Peter V'landys confirmed the plan would be to add three teams to the NRL by 2030, of which up to two could be based outside of Australia.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-38)

In October 2024 a [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth,_Western_Australia "Perth, Western Australia"), [Western Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Australia "Western Australia") bid, in consultation with the [North Sydney Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sydney_Bears "North Sydney Bears") and backed by the Western Australian Government, was reported however this was rejected 2 weeks later by the NRL commission over fears the consortium would be unable to fund the $20 million expansion fee.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-40) By November, talks had resumed and the Western Bears were largely expected to be announced as the NRL's 18th team, entering in the 2027 season.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-41)

On 12 December 2024, ARLC chairman [Peter V'landys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_V'landys "Peter V'landys"), Australian Prime Minister [Anthony Albanese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Albanese "Anthony Albanese") and Prime Minister [James Marape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Marape "James Marape") announced a team based in [Papua New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_New_Guinea "Papua New Guinea") would enter the NRL in the 2028 season. The $600 million venture is funded by the Australian Government for a ten-year period and was made in conjunction with a parallel agreement concerning "strategic trust" and security between the two countries. The team will be based in the capital city of [Port Moresby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Moresby "Port Moresby") and play home matches at the [National Football Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PNG_Football_Stadium "PNG Football Stadium").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-nrl.com-43) The bid would be partially funded by the Australian Government, providing $600M over 10 years to develop the competition in PNG[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-44)

Having selected a [Papua New Guinea NRL team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_New_Guinea_NRL_team "Papua New Guinea NRL team") as its eighteenth team, in April 2025, the NRL originally put negotiations on hold after deciding to postpone the introduction of a 19th team.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-45) However, by 24 April 2025, the NRL agreed to a $50 million deal with the Western Australian Government, thereby securing the 2027 return of the Bears as the [Perth Bears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth_Bears "Perth Bears").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-nrl-agrees-50m-deal-46)

Under the terms of the final agreement with the ARLC, the WA government has committed to spending a total of $85 million, including $35 million on grassroots rugby over the next seven years, with the remaining $50 million being $25 million on content over the next five years, $5 million to help with the costs of the new team, and $20 million will be committed to a Centre of Excellence. The WA government will not pay a licence fee, with a promise being made that there will be a likely upgrade of their home ground, the [Perth Rectangular Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth_Rectangular_Stadium "Perth Rectangular Stadium").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-nrl-agrees-50m-deal-46)

In May 2026, Abdo resigned from his role as CEO of the NRL while announcing a move to become CEO of [Tennis Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_Australia "Tennis Australia").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Rugby_League#cite_note-AbdoResign-47)
