**Footgolf** is a hybrid [sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport "Sport") in which players kick a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_(association_football) "Ball (association football)") (soccer ball) into a cup in as few shots as possible. The name is a [portmanteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portmanteau "Portmanteau") of [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") and [golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-rediff-2)

'FootGolf' is the name established by the [Federation for International FootGolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_for_International_FootGolf "Federation for International FootGolf") (FIFG) which governs, sets global standards, establishes rules and guidelines, and coordinates the sport’s development among its member associations.

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Rules")]

The game is played similarly to golf, with the exception that players use a football instead of a golf ball, and the ball is kicked rather than struck with a club,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-telegraph-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-4) working toward a 50 cm-52 cm diameter by 28 cm deep "footgolf cup" usually located away from golf greens.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-herald-5) The player who finishes the course with the fewest shots wins.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-info-6) Footgolf is often played on golf courses, though it may also be played on specially built courses. The first shot has to be played from a tee box, and bunkers, trees, water and hills must be crossed or avoided in order to reach the hole.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-info-6)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/FootGolf_Player_making_a_putt.jpg/250px-FootGolf_Player_making_a_putt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FootGolf_Player_making_a_putt.jpg)

Footgolf player making a putt

The game is played with a regulation No. 5 football.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-herald-5) Since footballs cannot be propelled as far as golf balls in one shot, footgolf is played on holes shorter than those used in golf.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-cnn-7)[Pars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Par_(score) "Par (score)") are typically five shots or fewer.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-herald-5) Compared to golf, footgolf is quicker to play, faster to learn, and cheaper in terms of equipment.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-telegraph-3)

The [Federation for International FootGolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_for_International_FootGolf "Federation for International FootGolf") (FIFG) has published a footgolf rulebook since 2012.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-8)

## Origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origins")]

A game with roughly similar rules, [codeball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codeball "Codeball"), attained brief popularity in the United States during the late 1920s and 1930s.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-11)The sport of footgolf as we know it today (including attire, etiquette and general rules) was created in the Netherlands in 2008 by Bas Korsten and Michael Jansen, who loosely based it on a post-training game played by Korsten's brother—pro-footballer [Willem Korsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_Korsten "Willem Korsten")—during his time at British football club [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur "Tottenham Hotspur") from 1999 to 2001. Players would end training sessions by kicking the footballs from the training pitch back to the changing rooms in as few kicks as possible. To officially launch this new sport, in which playing on a regulation golf course is fundamental, Korsten, Jansen and a team of colleagues set up a national and international bond and organised the first tournament (Nederlandse Kampioenschap FootGolf) at Golfbaan Het Rijk van Nijmegen on 6 September 2009. This tournament, later televised on RTL7, was played by Dutch professional and ex-professional footballers and won by Theo Janssen.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-cnn2-1)

In parallel, the sport also began developing in other regions. In September 2009, Francisco Name registered the trademark "Fut-Golf" with the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI), representing one of the earliest documented references to the sport in Latin America. The trademark later became associated with the development and organization of footgolf activities in Mexico.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-12)

## Organized play

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Organized play")]

The first-ever footgolf tournament was organized in the Netherlands by Michael Jansen and Bas Korsten,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-cnn2-1) and played by a mix of Dutch and Belgian professional footballers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-cnn2-1) After this, many countries began organizing matches, events, tournaments, national leagues and national associations around this game.

Later, Belgium and Hungary switched from playing in parks to golf courses,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and the game was introduced to Argentina in 2010.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-rediff-2) American FootGolf League, the major league of footgolf in the United States, was founded in 2011.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-utsd-13) The game was internationally publicized, and countries worldwide started collaborating on the development of the game. By 2014, the game was offered at hundreds of courses in the United States[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-herald-5) and was in the final stages of being recognized by [Sport England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_England "Sport England").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-telegraph-3)

The game's emergence coincided with the decline of the popularity of golf among young people, with 643 courses closing between 2006 and 2014 in the United States.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-cnn-7) The sport has saved many struggling golf courses,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-telegraph-3) and the [Professional Golfers' Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_Golfers'_Association_of_America "Professional Golfers' Association of America") and [World Golf Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Golf_Foundation "World Golf Foundation") have both acknowledged footgolf's contribution to helping golf courses generate more income, and noted that it may contribute to the growth of golf itself.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-pga-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-15) Former PGA president Ted Bishop said in 2014 that "I think it would be ludicrous to think there won't be a percentage of those people that might say, 'Hey, you know what? I think I'd like to try and play golf.'"[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-pga-14) In March 2016, the LPGA golfer [Paula Creamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Creamer "Paula Creamer") said "Anytime you can do something differently in the game of golf, it's fun and I think we'll probably be out there (playing FootGolf) a little bit more now."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball#cite_note-16) By 2020, the [State Games of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Games_of_America "State Games of America") and the USA Masters Games have included the sport of footgolf in their official competitions.[[17]](

##### FootGolf: The new kid on the block

Follow us at [@WorldSportCNN](https://twitter.com/WorldSportCNN) and [like us on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/worldsportcnn)

### Story highlights

FootGolf is played in a number of countries around the world

The Federation for International FootGolf boasts 22 member nations

UK FootGolf set to introduce its own UK FootGolf Academy Scheme

Why play one sport when you can play two at the same time?

That was the question a number of like-minded individuals were asking themselves, circa 2006.

And it is thanks to the vision of these select few that the sport of FootGolf – a game, unsurprisingly, combining elements of football and golf – was born and has been spreading its way around the globe ever since.

Ad Feedback

One of those men was Mike O’Connor, who today combines the roles of president of the [Federation for International FootGolf](http://www.fifg.org/) (FIFG) and president of [UK FootGolf](http://www.ukfootgolf.com/).

“I just knew FootGolf would be a bit of a no-brainer for the amount of golf courses there are, as well as the number of golfers and footballers,” O’Connor told CNN of a game that involves players kicking a football around a golf course, complete with bigger holes.

“I always thought it would take off. So it was just a question of waiting for the right time to get involved with it all really.”

After years in production, O’Connor would bring the sport to the UK – where there are now over 10,000 active players – and set up UK FootGolf in 2012.

Yet it is a Dutchman called Michael Jansen who is credited with the title of founding father of the game.

A lot of people are getting involved and loving the sport. It’s definitely the fun element that attracts people to it.

Mike O'Connor, FIFG president and UK FootGolf president

“He created what we do today,” O’Connor said. “He created everything, from how the game is played, down to the look of the players. Everything.”

**Kicking around a new idea**

Jansen, now an FIFG ambassador, held the first FootGolf competition in the Netherlands in 2008, after hearing of a unique idea from friend and former professional footballer Willem Korsten.

Korsten had played an early interpretation of the game during his days at Tottenham Hotspur, when he and his teammates would attempt to kick a football from the training pitch back to the changing rooms in as little time as possible.

The mere invention of FootGolf seems to be a natural progression, given that football and golf have long shared a close relationship.

Footballers are well known for playing golf in their spare time, so perhaps it is no surprise that FootGolf has proved such a hit with those hailing from a footballing background – 70% of people who have taken up the sport have been footballers.

While there is obviously the relaxing aspect of walking around a golf course on a sunny day, former English Premier League player Bryan Hughes also feels that the sport represents another opportunity for footballers to flex their competitive muscles.

“There is that challenge when playing golf. As sportsmen, we’ve all got that in our lockers. We want to challenge each other, we want to challenge ourselves and obviously be the best. That’s why footballers turn to golf,” he told CNN.

“It can be a challenge if you want, but I think it’s good that you can actually have it as a casual game as well. Some footballers play golf but do it as a hobby, to relax and wind down, and escape from the pressures of a football match on a Saturday.”

But while golf is in good health when it comes to attracting footballers, the sport has lost players in recent years – According to a report in [The New York Times](http://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/19/sports/golf/in-a-hole-golf-considers-digging-a-wider-one.html?ref=sports&_r=1), a recent survey by the U.S. National Golf Foundation estimated the game has lost five million in the last decade, with 20% of the existing 25 million golfers likely to quit in the next few years.

Many feel the game takes too long to play, is too difficult to learn and has too many complicated rules, which has led to a number of new alternatives being introduced to help boost a sport in decline.

Such concerns have led to the introduction on golf courses of 15 inch-wide holes – about four times the width of a standard hole – a relaxation in the game’s rules, and of course, FootGolf.

**Gaining a worldwide foothold**

Since Jansen’s inaugural competition – open to a mix of Dutch and Belgian professional footballers – the sport has gone from strength to strength.

Three countries formed the FIFG in June 2012 for the first ever World Cup in Budapest, Hungary, while today the world governing body boasts 22 different member nations, ranging from South Africa to Argentina.

“A lot of people are getting involved and loving the sport. It’s definitely the fun element that attracts people to it,” O’Connor said. “It catches such a large demographic because it’s such a low skill level to be able to play. You’ve just got to be able to kick a ball.”

And it is the sport’s ability to appeal to all that means a FootGolf course somewhere has likely played host to either a family visit, a first date, a corporate business trip or even, as was the case in the UK, an 81-year-old grandmother’s day out with her grandson.

But while there is little doubting the game’s capacity to attract members from most walks of life, O’Connor feels luring newcomers at a young age is truly pivotal to FootGolf’s future and its capability to grow as a sport.

“When I first set up FootGolf I knew a lot of people would want to play the sport, and I knew I wouldn’t be alone in liking the idea of playing football on a golf course,” he said. “But I was always conscious of the next level.

“I knew it would take off with adults, but we started looking at how the sport could continue to grow and grow. And if you get the youngsters involved you’re going to still be going in 10, 20, 30 years’ time, and you’ll be continuing to build, develop and progress.”

Much to O’Connor’s surprise, since its introduction, the sport seems to have struck a particular chord with junior football coaches.

There has been an overwhelming response from these coaches, who have contacted UK FootGolf to explain that the game is the perfect way to help youngsters focus on their passing and shooting.

So much so, that the governing body has taken the steps to set up its very own UK FootGolf Academy Scheme, due to start for business in May, and headed up by Hughes, who previously played for Birmingham City, Charlton Athletic and Hull City and is now a player-assistant manager at Scarborough Athletic.

In five years’ time, every country in the world that has got golf courses will be a member of the Federation for International FootGolf.

Mike O'Connor, FIFG president and UK FootGolf president

The scheme is currently being worked on with UK-based [1st4sport](http://www.1st4sport.com/) – who develop training qualifications for the likes of the English Football Association and the English Rugby Football Union – and will range from including holiday camps for kids to qualification courses for future coaches.

Hughes will take on the role of academy director, and like O’Connor, he feels the scheme can help to push the boundaries of FootGolf even further.

“The concept of FootGolf is something that really appeals to me and I’m sure there is a massive amount of people that would really want to get involved with the Academy Scheme. The potential there is huge and it is something that I’m really looking forward to,” Hughes said.

“I don’t think a lot of kids get the right sort of education when it comes to sport, I think they just want to kick the ball against a wall nowadays. They need direction and for somebody to really push them a little, to get them right up there and become the best they really can be. The scheme will give you that platform.”

As well as furthering the profile of the sport, the Academy Scheme will be hoping to produce some of the FootGolfers of tomorrow.

**A tour de force**

The FIGC currently stages a European Tour, with each of its different 22 member nations holding their own tournament throughout the year.

Some of the world’s finest players go from competition to competition looking to accumulate points, before a European champion is eventually crowned at the final stage in Portugal in November.

“Players travel from country to country because they love FootGolf and they love trying different courses,” O’Connor said. “There’s quite a small, but cult, following of people that do this. They all want to get ranked and be known as a good FootGolfer, not just in their own country but around the world.”

There are also a number of domestic tournaments taking place each year on various courses across the globe.

The U.S. currently leads the way when it comes to different courses with 90, while the UK, now boasting 30, has made impressive progress to move up to second, given it had just two at the beginning of 2013.

With FootGolf continuing to make huge strides both at home and abroad, O’Connor has high hopes for the sport and feels the sky is most certainly the limit.

“In five years’ time, every country in the world that has got golf courses will be a member of the Federation for International FootGolf,” O’Connor said. “With the amount of inquiries we are getting from all over the place, I have no doubt about that.

“We’ve got somebody in Togo asking us about joining the FIFG. They’ve only got one golf course in Togo, and they’re talking about putting FootGolf on it! That’s how big an impact the sport is having around the world.”

# What Is FootGolf?

FootGolf is a sport that plays out exactly like golf: same course, same par, same 18 holes, except instead of clubs and a small dimpled ball, players kick a standard soccer ball toward an oversized hole.

## The basic concept

A round of FootGolf follows the structure of golf almost exactly. Courses use tee boxes, fairways, bunkers, and hazards, and each hole has a designated par. Instead of a golf ball and clubs, players kick a size 5 soccer ball from the tee, continuing to kick from wherever it comes to rest until it drops into a hole 50 to 52 cm (about 20 inches) across (per the FIFG rulebook), nearly five times the diameter of a standard golf hole. You may also see it written as["football golf", "foot golf" or "soccer golf"](https://footgolfsport.com/blog/what-is-football-golf-called), which are informal names for the same sport.

Scoring works identically to golf: your score is the number of kicks it takes to complete a hole, and that number is compared to par using the same familiar terms: birdie, bogey, eagle, and so on.

## Where FootGolf came from

Kicking a ball around a golf course wasn't a brand-new idea in 2008 (informal versions had popped up in a few countries earlier), but that year is generally treated as the sport's real starting point. **Bas Korsten and Michael Jansen**created the sport in the Netherlands in 2008, putting standardized rules, hole sizes, and scoring behind what had previously been a casual pastime. The first official tournament followed in September 2009, according to[USA FootGolf](https://www.usafootgolf.org/about). Our[short history of FootGolf](https://footgolfsport.com/blog/who-invented-footgolf-history)has the full timeline.

From there, growth was fast. Within a few years, national FootGolf associations had formed across Europe, and the sport crossed the Atlantic soon after, taking hold on courses across the United States.

## How FootGolf is governed today

FootGolf has real organizational structure behind it, which is a big part of why it's treated as a legitimate sport rather than a novelty activity:

*   **Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG)**: the international governing body, responsible for the standardized rulebook and the[FootGolf World Cup](https://footgolfsport.com/blog/footgolf-world-cup-history-and-winners)between national teams.
*   **American FootGolf League (AFGL)**: the US governing organization, which affiliates and approves FootGolf courses, sets a player code of conduct, and runs a season-long competitive tour.

Want the details on the AFGL specifically?[Read our full breakdown of the league](https://footgolfsport.com/blog/american-footgolf-league-explained). Outside the US, national federations like the UK FootGolf Association and the FootGolf Association of Ireland play the same role. See our guide to[FootGolf courses in the UK and Ireland](https://footgolfsport.com/footgolf-courses-in-the-uk).

## FootGolf vs. golf: the short version

The course and scoring are nearly identical; the equipment and skill set are not. Golf tests swing mechanics and club selection across a bag of specialized clubs. FootGolf tests kicking technique and distance control with a single ball, which makes it dramatically cheaper and faster to learn. For a full side-by-side comparison, see[FootGolf vs. Golf: What's Actually Different?](https://footgolfsport.com/blog/footgolf-vs-golf-differences)

## Why FootGolf keeps growing

FootGolf solves a real problem for golf courses: it opens up an existing asset (the course) to a completely new, lower-cost audience without competing for tee times in the same way. For players, it offers the outdoor, social, competitive experience of golf without the steep equipment cost or learning curve, which is why so many courses now run FootGolf alongside their traditional golf operations.

## Frequently asked questions

What is FootGolf?FootGolf is a sport that combines soccer and golf. Players kick a soccer ball around a golf course, aiming to get it into a large hole in as few kicks as possible, following the same par-based scoring system used in golf.

Who invented FootGolf?Organized FootGolf is widely credited to Bas Korsten and Michael Jansen, who created the sport in the Netherlands in 2008 and set its rules, building on informal kicking games that had been played for years.

Who governs FootGolf?The Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG) governs the sport internationally, including the FIFG World Cup. In the United States, the American FootGolf League (AFGL) governs sanctioned courses and tournaments.

Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG) has been advancing and developing [FootGolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf "Footgolf") as a standardised global sport since 2012. Headquartered in Lausanne, Switzerland, FIFG promotes the global recognition and development of FootGolf, establishes and enforces standardised international rules, organises major competitions (including the FIFG World Cup, FIFG World Tour and FIFG Regional Tours), and regulates national member associations.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_for_International_FootGolf&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

**Origins and early variants**

For decades, games conceptually similar to FootGolf were played informally across the globe on beaches, farms, parks, and other open spaces. These informal variants emerged under a variety of local names, including [Codeball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codeball "Codeball"), Footballgolf, foot-golf, Futgolf, Soccer-Golf, Kick-golf, Footee, and [Buschball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buschball "Buschball") and operated under localised rules that often differed significantly from one another.

The modern standardised format of the game emerged in the Netherlands between 2008 and 2010 when Michael Jansen and Bas Korsten developed a rule set based on traditional golf. They subsequently organised the world’s first official tournament on a regulation golf course, establishing the foundational template that would later be adopted globally.

**The International FootGolf Association and structural challenges**

Although Michael Jansen and his business partners intended to lay the initial foundations for international governance by creating the International FootGolf Association (IFGA) during the 2009-2010 period, the transition from a localised concept into a structured international sport proved exceptionally difficult. Due to the overwhelming financial burdens of global distances and restrictive economics, the IFGA went dormant. To end confusion and potential organisational rivalries and unite the sport under a single banner, the IFGA officially recognised the Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG) as the sole global governing body for the sport. The FIFG recognised Michael Jansen as a co‑creator of the basic modern rules of the sport as it is played today and serves the organisation as an FIFG Ambassador and Honorary Board Member. [CNN](https://edition.cnn.com/2014/04/28/sport/golf/footgolf)

**Foundation and growth of the FIFG**

The Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG) was formally established in 2012 by sports enthusiasts who united their resources to create a unified global governing body. The federation was publicly announced in June 2012 during the inaugural FootGolf World Cup held near Budapest, Hungary. Today the FIFG maintains its international headquarters at Place Saint‑François 7, 1003 Lausanne, Switzerland. While casual FootGolf is estimated to be played in over one hundred countries, the regulated competitive sport is strictly organised by multiple member countries under the FIFG framework.

**Founding**

The FIFG was founded by Roberto Balestrini, Laura Balestrini, and Francisco Gonzalez Briones from FIFG Region 1 – North America; Javier de Ancizar from FIFG Region 2 – South America; and Gábor Gelencser, Mauritz van Tubergen, and Leonardo Decaria from FIFG Region 3 – Europe. Working together to establish the FIFG as the sport’s international governing body, they coordinated with Hungary's Gábor Gelencser to host the first FIFG FootGolf World Cup near Budapest in June 2012, which featured 126 excited players from eight countries.

## Name and branding

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_for_International_FootGolf&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Name and branding")]

The Federation for International FootGolf adopted and standardised the sport’s name under it's brand as a single word with a capital F and a capital G: FootGolf. Accordingly, the sport governed by FIFG rules and guidelines is officially identified as FootGolf, and the Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG) promotes the sport under this trademarked title, having published and periodically updated an official rulebook since 2012 to ensure uniform rules worldwide.

## Structure and leadership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_for_International_FootGolf&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Structure and leadership")]

FIFG is governed by a Board of Directors, which functions as the central decision-making body responsible for strategic direction, policy development, and oversight of the sport’s global administration. The board approves key initiatives, including rules and policies, through convened meetings where members deliberate on matters such as competition structures, membership criteria, and organisational reforms.

The board comprises defined leadership roles: President – leads overall operations and represents FIFG internationally 1st Vice President and 2nd Vice President – assist in executive duties and chair specific initiatives General Secretary – manages administrative affairs, including correspondence and record-keeping Treasurer – oversees financial matters Additional board members and advisors

Past presidents: Javier de Ancizar, Mauritz van Tubergen, Michael O'Connor, Roberto Balestrini, Gabor Gelencser, Laura Balestrini. Current president: Aleksander Kravanja

On October 3, 2017, the [Global Association of International Sports Federations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Association_of_International_Sports_Federations "Global Association of International Sports Federations") announced the federation as one of the first international federations to achieve Observer status.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_for_International_FootGolf#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_for_International_FootGolf#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_for_International_FootGolf#cite_note-3)

That year also saw the introduction of FIFG Regional Majors and ranked tournaments, such as the FIFG 500 series, to promote sustained player development and event diversity across continents.

## Core responsibilities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_for_International_FootGolf&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Core responsibilities")]

Rule Standardisation: Establishes and maintains the Official FIFG Rulebook, guidelines, and player codes of conduct to guarantee consistent gameplay worldwide.

Global Tournaments: Organises the premier international competitions for the sport, including the official FootGolf Tours and the multi-category FootGolf World Cup.

National Affiliation: Dictates membership frameworks, recognising only one exclusive national organisation per country to govern local play.

Dispute Resolution: Exercises sole jurisdiction over resolving institutional conflicts or administrative disagreements between member countries or continental federations.

Sport Integrity & Anti-Doping: Protects the integrity of the sport by mandating strict ethical guidelines, combating corruption, and delivering anti-doping programmes in partnership with the International Testing Agency] ([ITA](https://ita.sport/partner/federation-for-international-footgolf-fifg/)).

Inclusivity & Growth: Sets mandatory criteria for its member nations to expand the sport at the grassroots level, specifically promoting the inclusion of women, youth, and athletes with disabilities.

## Members

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_for_International_FootGolf&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Members")]

The Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG) recognises only one exclusive member per [country](https://www.footgolf.sport/countries/). Membership is restricted to a single national organisation that serves as the official governing body for the sport within its territory. Players are required to affiliate with the FIFG member organisation of their country of birth or permanent residence. Unrepresented countries may apply to initiate the formal membership process. To achieve official recognition, an applicant national organisation must satisfy requirements across four primary categories: governance, universality, ethics, and responsibility.

**Governance**

. Institutional Structure: The applicant must be a legally registered national organisation governed by a general assembly as its supreme decision‑making body.

. Administrative Principles: Organizations must implement principles of good governance, including transparency, accountability, gender equity, non‑discrimination, and institutional fairness.

**Universality and Development**

. Domestic Competition: The organisation must actively develop the sport by hosting a minimum of three tournaments annually, distributed across at least two distinct golf courses.

. International Integration: Scheduled events must attract a significant field of competitive players who are formally affiliated with existing FIFG member countries.

**Ethics and Responsibility**

. Inclusivity and Safety: Member organisations must promote inclusive participation—specifically for women and individuals with disabilities, while supporting "sport for all" initiatives. They are required to uphold high-standard officiating, clear competition rules, fair play, and athlete health and safety protocols.

. Anti-Doping Compliance: The organisation must be a signatory to the World Anti‑Doping Code, maintain domestic anti‑doping regulations aligned with the Code, and actively participate in anti-doping initiatives.

. Integrity Safeguards: Organisations must implement formal frameworks to protect athletes and sports personnel from corruption, fraudulent activities, illegal or irregular sports betting, and other malicious practices.

The combined criteria ensure that each recognised national federation operates with high institutional integrity, fosters inclusive growth, and strictly aligns with international standards for clean and ethical sport.

## Player Affiliations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_for_International_FootGolf&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Player Affiliations")]

Players are not FIFG Members. A player may affiliate to only one [FIFG Member Country](https://www.footgolf.sport/countries/) by citizenship or residence.

Players from countries with a non-active member must contact the FIFG and complete the form requesting to join official competitions. [FORM](https://www.footgolf.sport/players/)

## FIFG FootGolf World Cup

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_for_International_FootGolf&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: FIFG FootGolf World Cup")]

The FIFG FootGolf World Cup is the premier international tournament for the sport of FootGolf, which combines elements of soccer and golf. The championship brings together the best FootGolf players from around the world to compete in different categories, including men’s individual, women’s individual, seniors, and national team events (national selections).

The 1st FIFG World Cup was played in Budapest, Hungary, in June 2012, organised by the FootGolf Hungary. It featured 126 players from eight countries: Argentina, Belgium, Greece, Hungary, Italy, Mexico, the Netherlands, and the United States.

The 2nd FIFG FootGolf World Cup was held in January 2016 in Pilar (Buenos Aires Province) Argentina. Organised by the Asociación Argentina de FootGolf, the event hosted over 230 players from 26 FIFG member countries.

The 3rd FIFG FootGolf World Cup, organised by the French FootGolf Association, was played in Marrakesh, Morocco in 2018 and attracted 520 players from 33 countries.

The 4th FIFG FootGolf World Cup was organised by the American FootGolf Federation in 2023 in [Orlando](https://www.orlando2023.com/), Florida, United States. The event brought together 972 players from 39 countries.

The 5th FIFG FootGolf World Cup was organised by the Federación Mexicana de FootGolf in [Acapulco](https://www.footgolf.sport/acapulcoworldcup2026/), Mexico, in 2026. The tournament gathered more than 1,200 players from over 60 countries and 64 national teams across all categories, making it the largest edition in the competition’s history.

## FIFG Youth FootGolf

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Federation_for_International_FootGolf&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: FIFG Youth FootGolf")]

The inaugural [FIFG Youth FootGolf World Cup](https://www.footgolf.sport/youthworldcupgermany2026/) was played in Germany in 2026.

In 2025 American FootGolf League worked with the NJ Youth Soccer Association and Crystal Springs Resort to launch a FootGolf championship for youth in New Jersey. In 2026, the NJYSA expands the second annual [Youth FootGolf Championship](https://www.njyouthsoccer.com/news/njys-footgolf-championships-2026/) successfully and introduced interactive activities for both parents and friends.

The American FootGolf League launched the [U.S. Youth FootGolf Development Program](https://www.footgolfusa.com/youth) to expand the game to youth across the United States, including supporting programmes that target players with disabilities. [Home](https://everykickcounts.org/)

**Footgolf** is a hybrid [sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport "Sport") in which players kick a [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_(association_football) "Ball (association football)") (soccer ball) into a cup in as few shots as possible. The name is a [portmanteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portmanteau "Portmanteau") of [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") and [golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-rediff-2)

'FootGolf' is the name established by the [Federation for International FootGolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_for_International_FootGolf "Federation for International FootGolf") (FIFG) which governs, sets global standards, establishes rules and guidelines, and coordinates the sport’s development among its member associations.

## Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Rules")]

The game is played similarly to golf, with the exception that players use a football instead of a golf ball, and the ball is kicked rather than struck with a club,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-telegraph-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-4) working toward a 50 cm-52 cm diameter by 28 cm deep "footgolf cup" usually located away from golf greens.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-herald-5) The player who finishes the course with the fewest shots wins.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-info-6) Footgolf is often played on golf courses, though it may also be played on specially built courses. The first shot has to be played from a tee box, and bunkers, trees, water and hills must be crossed or avoided in order to reach the hole.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-info-6)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/43/FootGolf_Player_making_a_putt.jpg/250px-FootGolf_Player_making_a_putt.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:FootGolf_Player_making_a_putt.jpg)

Footgolf player making a putt

The game is played with a regulation No. 5 football.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-herald-5) Since footballs cannot be propelled as far as golf balls in one shot, footgolf is played on holes shorter than those used in golf.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-cnn-7)[Pars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Par_(score) "Par (score)") are typically five shots or fewer.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-herald-5) Compared to golf, footgolf is quicker to play, faster to learn, and cheaper in terms of equipment.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-telegraph-3)

The [Federation for International FootGolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_for_International_FootGolf "Federation for International FootGolf") (FIFG) has published a footgolf rulebook since 2012.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-8)

## Origins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Origins")]

A game with roughly similar rules, [codeball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codeball "Codeball"), attained brief popularity in the United States during the late 1920s and 1930s.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-11)The sport of footgolf as we know it today (including attire, etiquette and general rules) was created in the Netherlands in 2008 by Bas Korsten and Michael Jansen, who loosely based it on a post-training game played by Korsten's brother—pro-footballer [Willem Korsten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_Korsten "Willem Korsten")—during his time at British football club [Tottenham Hotspur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tottenham_Hotspur "Tottenham Hotspur") from 1999 to 2001. Players would end training sessions by kicking the footballs from the training pitch back to the changing rooms in as few kicks as possible. To officially launch this new sport, in which playing on a regulation golf course is fundamental, Korsten, Jansen and a team of colleagues set up a national and international bond and organised the first tournament (Nederlandse Kampioenschap FootGolf) at Golfbaan Het Rijk van Nijmegen on 6 September 2009. This tournament, later televised on RTL7, was played by Dutch professional and ex-professional footballers and won by Theo Janssen.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-cnn2-1)

In parallel, the sport also began developing in other regions. In September 2009, Francisco Name registered the trademark "Fut-Golf" with the Mexican Institute of Industrial Property (IMPI), representing one of the earliest documented references to the sport in Latin America. The trademark later became associated with the development and organization of footgolf activities in Mexico.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-12)

## Organized play

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Organized play")]

The first-ever footgolf tournament was organized in the Netherlands by Michael Jansen and Bas Korsten,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-cnn2-1) and played by a mix of Dutch and Belgian professional footballers.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-cnn2-1) After this, many countries began organizing matches, events, tournaments, national leagues and national associations around this game.

Later, Belgium and Hungary switched from playing in parks to golf courses,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and the game was introduced to Argentina in 2010.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-rediff-2) American FootGolf League, the major league of footgolf in the United States, was founded in 2011.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-utsd-13) The game was internationally publicized, and countries worldwide started collaborating on the development of the game. By 2014, the game was offered at hundreds of courses in the United States[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-herald-5) and was in the final stages of being recognized by [Sport England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_England "Sport England").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-telegraph-3)

The game's emergence coincided with the decline of the popularity of golf among young people, with 643 courses closing between 2006 and 2014 in the United States.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-cnn-7) The sport has saved many struggling golf courses,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-telegraph-3) and the [Professional Golfers' Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professional_Golfers'_Association_of_America "Professional Golfers' Association of America") and [World Golf Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Golf_Foundation "World Golf Foundation") have both acknowledged footgolf's contribution to helping golf courses generate more income, and noted that it may contribute to the growth of golf itself.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-pga-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-15) Former PGA president Ted Bishop said in 2014 that "I think it would be ludicrous to think there won't be a percentage of those people that might say, 'Hey, you know what? I think I'd like to try and play golf.'"[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-pga-14) In March 2016, the LPGA golfer [Paula Creamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Creamer "Paula Creamer") said "Anytime you can do something differently in the game of golf, it's fun and I think we'll probably be out there (playing FootGolf) a little bit more now."[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-16) By 2020, the [State Games of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Games_of_America "State Games of America") and the USA Masters Games have included the sport of footgolf in their official competitions.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-18)

A group of countries combined to form the [Federation for International FootGolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_for_International_FootGolf "Federation for International FootGolf") (FIFG) in June 2012,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-cnn2-1) and eight countries played the first FootGolf World Cup in [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary") that month (won by Hungarian, Bela Lengyel). In January 2016, the second FootGolf World Cup was held in Argentina and 230 players from 26 FIFG member countries participated. The winner of the individual event was Argentinian player, Christian Otero and the team champion was Team USA. The third FootGolf World Cup was held in December 2018, in Marrakech, Morocco. The men's individual champion was Matias Perrone from Argentina and the women's individual champion was Sophie Brown from the United Kingdom. France won the gold in team competition, Team UK finished second and the previous world champion Team USA finished in third.

In the spring of 2015, the National Golf Courses Owners Association (NGCOA) recognized the American FootGolf League (AFGL) as the governing body for the sport of footgolf in the U.S.,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-19) and a few months later, Roberto Balestrini, founder of footgolf in North America was selected by _Golf Inc Magazine_ as one of "The Ten Most Innovative People in Golf".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-20) On 2 October 2017, the GAISF ([Global Association of International Sports Federations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_Association_of_International_Sports_Federations "Global Association of International Sports Federations")) granted [observer status](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observer_status "Observer status") to the Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG).[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-21)

In December 2015,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-22) the [Swedish Golf Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Golf_Federation "Swedish Golf Federation"), a member of the highest sporting authority in Sweden (the [Swedish Sports Confederation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_Sports_Confederation "Swedish Sports Confederation")), by a formal two-part voting, accepted and approved footgolf as an official sport (eligible for recognition in national championships, future inclusion in the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games"), etc.).

The fourth FIFG FootGolf World Cup took place in Orlando, Florida in 2023 and displayed its global reach with trophies won by six countries in individual and team competitions.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-23) It was held at [Walt Disney World](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walt_Disney_World "Walt Disney World") Golf Resort and the Evermore Orlando Resort from 27 May through 6 June. Nearly 1,000 professional footgolf players from 39 countries gathered for the event, including former professional athletes like [Alan Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Smith_(footballer,_born_1980) "Alan Smith (footballer, born 1980)"), [Olindo Mare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olindo_Mare "Olindo Mare"), and [Roberto Ayala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Ayala "Roberto Ayala").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-25) It was broadcast on ESPN.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-26)

In 2023, The Professional Footgolf Tour staged the first international footgolf event in the Middle East when the Sharjah International FootGolf event took place in January of that year. The event, hosted by the Sharjah Commerce and Tourism Development Authority, offered a $40,000 prize fund to be shared between the winning players. This event was part of the Sharjah's 'Week of the Stars' event, where football legends such as Francesco Totti, Clarence Seedorf and Alessandro Costacurta have also played the game.

Mexico emerged as one of the leading footgolf nations in Latin America during the 2010s and 2020s, developing a national competitive structure and hosting annual championships through the Mexican FootGolf Federation. Footgolf competitions are held in numerous Mexican cities, including Acapulco, Cancún, Guadalajara, León, Monterrey, Puebla, Veracruz and Mexico City.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-27)

In 2026, Acapulco hosted the 5th FIFG FootGolf World Cup. The event brought together more than 1,200 players from over 60 countries and 64 national teams, marking a significant milestone in the sport's global expansion and represented the largest FootGolf championship staged in Latin America and the world.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-28)

## Buschball

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Buschball")]

Buschball is a variation invented in Germany.

### Rules

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Rules")]

The aim of the game is to hit the pole with as few shots as possible. The pole is a [flag pole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flagpole_(structure)#Flagpoles "Flagpole (structure)"). Both the pole as well as the flag are part of the target.

First the order of the players is drawn. The first player sets the pole for the first round, the second player begins the round by trying to hit the pole with as few kicks as possible. Once everyone has had a turn the second player places the pole and the third player starts the round etc.

Every player has a maximum of nine attempts to hit the pole. If after these nine attempts he fails to hit the pole ten points are recorded for that particular player and it is the following player's turn. At the end of the round the player with the fewest kicks is awarded a best round.

The first set is completed once everyone has had a turn to place the pole. The players can decide how many sets they wish to play. The winner is the person who at the end of the last set has the fewest kicks. In the case of a draw the number of best rounds decides.  
 Note: While playing, no-one is allowed to touch the ball while it is still moving. Before a shot, any loose object behind the ball (sticks, stones, etc.) can be removed to ensure safety. Any object in front of the ball may not be removed.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-30)

### History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: History")]

The oldest known version of buschball was played in 1977.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-31) Due to a lack of players for a standard game of football Andreas Oligmüller and his friends decided to shoot at trees and [road signs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_signs "Road signs"). After a while that became too easy so they decided to aim at trees hidden behind bushes. The first variant of the game was born.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-32)

### Players and clubs

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Footgolf&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Players and clubs")]

The number of players and clubs is constantly growing. In 2008, 35 people played buschball and in 2009 the sport had managed to attract 150 players.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Footgolf#cite_note-33)

# FootGolf: The Sport Where You Kick Your Way Around 18 Holes

FootGolf is real golf, played with your feet. Swap the clubs for a soccer ball, keep the same scorecard, and play one of the fastest-growing sports in the country, on courses you already know.

## What Is FootGolf?

FootGolf takes the layout, etiquette, and scoring of golf and swaps the clubs and small ball for a soccer ball and your feet. Players kick from a tee box toward a hole about 20 inches (50 to 52 cm) wide cut into the green, using the same par, bunkers, hazards, and 18-hole structure as traditional golf.

Organized FootGolf is widely credited to Bas Korsten and Michael Jansen, who created the sport in the Netherlands in 2008. The sport has since spread to dozens of countries and is now governed internationally by the Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG), with the American FootGolf League (AFGL)overseeing sanctioned courses and tournaments across the United States.

[Read the full history and explanation](https://footgolfsport.com/what-is-footgolf)

![Image 2: Close-up of a soccer ball resting beside an oversized FootGolf hole on the green](https://footgolfsport.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpicsum.photos%2Fseed%2Ffootgolfsport-oversized-hole%2F900%2F700&w=3840&q=75)

## Why People Are Falling For FootGolf

![Image 3: A group of friends walking the fairway during a FootGolf round](https://footgolfsport.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpicsum.photos%2Fseed%2Ffootgolfsport-group-round%2F900%2F700&w=1920&q=75)

Genuine Competition

Behind the casual vibe is a real competitive scene: sanctioned AFGL tour stops, national rankings, and a FIFG World Cup.

### Easy To Learn

If you can kick a ball, you can play. There's no swing to master, so it's approachable for total beginners and families alike.

### A Real Workout

An 18-hole round means miles of walking plus the balance and accuracy of a controlled kick, good cardio dressed up as a laid-back afternoon.

## How To Play FootGolf

FootGolf follows the same flow as a round of golf: play in groups set by the course (commonly up to four players), moving through the holes in order. Full rules, scoring, group etiquette, and technique tips for your first round are covered in our complete guide.

1.   1
Tee off

Start with the ball inside the tee zone at the tee markers.

2.   2
Play it as it lies

Keep kicking from wherever the ball stops, without improving your lie.

3.   3
Mind the flag

You can have the flagstick removed, but nobody may hold it while you kick.

4.   4
Hole out

The round ends when the ball drops into the cup; write down your score.

[See the full rules & scoring guide](https://footgolfsport.com/how-to-play-footgolf)

## What To Wear & Bring

Most FootGolf courses enforce the same dress code as their golf side: collared shirts, golf shorts or pants, and turf or indoor soccer shoes instead of cleats. Bring your own approved ball if you have one, a towel, and sunscreen for a full 18.

*   Collared shirt
*   Golf shorts, pants, or skirt
*   Turf or indoor soccer shoes
*   Approved size 5 FootGolf ball

## Find FootGolf Courses Near You

FootGolf courses now operate in nearly every US region, from dedicated facilities to traditional golf courses that added a FootGolf layout. We break down how to find a sanctioned course near you and how AFGL affiliation works.

[Start Your Course Search](https://footgolfsport.com/find-footgolf-courses-near-me)

## Common Questions

A few things almost everyone asks before their first round.

[Browse all FootGolf FAQs and articles](https://footgolfsport.com/blog)

What is FootGolf?FootGolf is a hybrid sport that combines soccer and golf. Players kick a soccer ball around a golf course and try to get it into an oversized hole in as few kicks as possible, using standard golf scoring (par, birdie, bogey, etc.).

Is FootGolf a real, organized sport?Yes. FootGolf is organized internationally by the Federation for International FootGolf (FIFG) and in the United States by the American FootGolf League (AFGL), which run sanctioned tournaments and maintain official rules.

Do I need special equipment to play FootGolf?You need a size 5 soccer ball approved for FootGolf play and comfortable athletic or turf shoes. Most courses provide or sell approved balls, so equipment costs to get started are minimal.

By [![Image 1: Kyle Feldscher](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/181129112952-kyle-feldscher-byline.jpg?c=16x9&q=h_270,w_480,c_fill/c_thumb,g_face,w_50,h_50)](https://www.cnn.com/profiles/kyle-feldscher)[Kyle Feldscher](https://www.cnn.com/profiles/kyle-feldscher)

![Image 2: Garrett Clark, co-founder of Good Good, is featured in the controversial driver ad.](https://media.cnn.com/api/v1/images/stellar/prod/gettyimages-2231193856.jpg?c=original&q=w_860,c_fill)

Garrett Clark, co-founder of Good Good, is featured in the controversial driver ad.

Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images

Atlanta—

The normally buttoned-up [world of golf](https://www.cnn.com/sport/golf) is dealing with its latest collision between traditional sensibilities and new age internet culture – and this time it’s putting into question how and whether those two worlds merge.

The golf-focused media company Good Good and equipment maker Callaway are both under fire this week after the release of an advertisement for a new co-branded driver featuring personalities from Good Good. [The ad started with a shocking image](https://x.com/FOS/status/2091574282472349876) of Garrett Clark, one of the co-founders of Good Good, shoulder-checking Alexis Miestowski to the ground as she went to touch his driver.

The advertisement quickly drew immense backlash and was pulled down, with Callaway and Good Good both facing intense questions over how an ad showing a violent act against a woman would be approved and posted.

Amid the backlash, Clark apologized for his “role” in the ad, and on behalf on Good Good, in a [video posted](https://x.com/gm__golf/status/2092759034533212412) to his X account on Wednesday night.

“This is not, at all, what we stand for. The way this ad was received is not how Good Good is and not what we stand for once again. I want everyone to know that. I do not support (domestic violence), abuse or any of that.”

Clark offered “some clarity” on the idea behind the ad, likening it to the 2026 movie “[Obsession](https://www.cnn.com/2026/06/07/entertainment/gen-z-horror-backrooms-obsession)” directed by 26-year-old YouTuber Curry Barker.

Clark explained that, like the movie, he was supposed to be obsessed with his driver and anybody who touched it, would become “possessed with the obsession.”

“Looking back, super dumb ad concept,” Clark added. “Terrible ad in general. Not the greatest idea. … Once I watched it back and it got posted, my skin was crawling. I was cringing. I mean, even just minutes after I saw it get posted, before this surfaced anywhere online, I thought it was the worst ad known to man.”

Clark described the comments and criticism the ad received as “very justified,” but denounced the hate and death threats Miestowski has received in her social media direct messages.

“If you got hate to give, got any left in the tank, give Good Good some hate. You can give me some hate in the comments down below. I do sincerely apologize for playing the role in the ad,” Clark said.

Clark said Good Good’s mission has always been to grow the game, and “not just within the male side of golf” with the addition of Good Good Girls.

“Golf has historically been and is a big male sport. And we have wanted to change that by including women in all of our content and pushing the women’s side of the game,” he said.

“Hopefully you guys can forgive Good Good as well as myself for being a part of it. And hopefully, we can move on and continue to grow the women’s side of golf.”

On Tuesday, Callaway CEO Chip Brewer admitted his company approved the ad and apologized for that mistake.
